title: Public Interest Data Science
text:
Preface
This is a book about doing data science for ends the public can name, contest, and use.
You already know, or will shortly, that most data science is not that. It produces things for an employer to ship, a platform to monetize, or a manager to track. When it produces things for the public, it tends to produce dashboards: objects that look like accountability without being accountable to anyone in particular. This book is written for the student who has noticed the gap between what data science can do and what it typically does, and who wants a way in that is neither naive about the tools nor resigned about the politics.

title: Public Interest Data Science
text:
Who this book is for
If you are a student taking a data-science course, a journalism or policy student learning computational methods, a working practitioner considering a move into civic or public-interest work, an instructor looking for a course companion, or a public-sector analyst being asked to do “data-driven” work with no time to read the entire literature, this book is for you. It assumes introductory Python, comfort with the command line, and a willingness to read ten pages about a court case before writing the function that acts on it. It does not assume a background in science and technology studies, law, or accounting. It will give you enough of each to keep going.
You can read it straight through, pick chapters relevant to a specific project, or use it as a course text. The chapters are written to be read out of order. The companion course, INFO 4871/5871 Public Interest Data Science at the University of Colorado Boulder, assigns them that way: each of its modules pairs one lineage with one pressure, one value, and one genre drawn from different parts of the book.

title: Public Interest Data Science
text:
What the book does
The book rests on a framework from Keegan (2026). Three structural pressures narrow the public’s capacity to observe and govern data-intensive systems: enclosure (who can observe?), exemption (who must answer?), and erosion (what can be remembered?). Three values push back: openness, oversight, and ownership. Values last only when they are built into an installed base with six elements: linkability, interpretability, continuity, safe scrutiny, authority, and remedy.
The book has five parts:

Pressures and Values (1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science to 5  Erosion and Ownership). The contested idea of “the public interest”; the installed base and its intellectual predecessors; and three paired chapters, each setting a pressure against the value that answers it.
Lineages (6  Journalism to 10  Engineering). What data scientists can inherit from journalism, law, accounting, planning, and engineering, and where each inheritance fails.
Adjacent Conversations (11  Public Interest Technology and Data for Good to 13  Critical Data Studies, Data Justice, and Refusal). Public interest technology, data for good, GovTech, civic tech, critical data studies, data justice, and refusal.
Genres (14  Op-Eds to 19  Archival Deposits). The forms through which data scientists contribute to public conversations: op-eds, reports, research proposals, testimony, public comments, and archival deposits.
Closing (20  The Limits of the Framework). The limits of the framework itself.

Lineages and genres each have a natural level of government, and the worked examples follow it: journalism and op-eds at the city; planning and public comments at the county; law and testimony at the state; accounting, engineering, and reports at the nation.

title: Public Interest Data Science
text:
How the book is built
Every chapter interweaves conceptual narrative with runnable Python tutorials at roughly a 50/50 balance. You will read two or three pages of argument, then read and run two or three pages of code that makes the argument visible in a specific case, then return to the argument. This is deliberate. Concepts without technique produce earnest seminars. Technique without concepts produces dashboards that nobody trusts.
Code blocks do not run at build time. They are illustrative: you are expected to type them, adapt them, and run them yourself. The book’s repository contains test fixtures, sample data, and the occasional larger notebook that a chapter only excerpts. When a chapter uses a real API (Wikimedia pageviews, regulations.gov, the Internet Archive), the endpoints cited were live as of the book’s most recent release; if you find one that has moved, open an issue.
Every chapter has at least one “Missing Manual” callout flagging something that textbooks usually omit: a surprising library default, a real-world API friction, the politics of a “simple” choice. Every chapter has at least one “In the Public Interest” callout tying the technical material back to openness, oversight, or ownership. Every chapter ends with 4–5 graduated exercises, from guided (“follow these steps”) to open-ended (“design a pipeline that…”), and a curated list of further resources.
Chapters in Part IV have one additional rule: they must end with a real submittable artifact. Not a thought experiment. An actual op-ed, report section, proposal page, testimony statement, public comment on a live matter, or archival deposit with a DOI, each paired with a technical artifact someone else can run. A reader who finishes Part IV has a portfolio.

title: Public Interest Data Science
text:
Running examples
To give the book coherence across 20 chapters, a small set of running examples is threaded throughout, arranged by level of government. When a chapter needs a case, it reaches for one of these before inventing a new one:

City: City of Boulder and City and County of Denver records (campaign finance, meeting minutes, agendas, budgets, permits, 311 requests).
County: Boulder County as planner and record keeper: land use matters, planning documents, and records already released under the Colorado Open Records Act (from the Public Records Archive of its Open Records Center).
State: Colorado law as rule maker: the Colorado Open Records Act, the Colorado AI Act, and the General Assembly.
Nation: national data from the American Community Survey (via folktables), federal automated decision systems, federal environmental and scientific data (EPA, NOAA, USGS, Census) as at-risk datasets, and regulations.gov for federal rulemaking.
Census and FRED APIs for demographic and economic context.
Wikipedia and Internet Archive APIs for archival work and link-rot audits.
Hugging Face model cards and datasheets for audit and documentation exercises.
A small synthetic worker-log fixture that lets us teach audit methods without violating anyone’s privacy.
Public FOIA and CORA request data as a class-wide shared resource.

By the end of the book you will have built, in parts, a small public-interest data infrastructure of your own: a reproduced investigation and a documented city dataset; an erosion audit and a stewardship plan or refusal specification; a ledger of exemptions and remedies; a tested, disaggregated audit; and the public texts that carry them (an op-ed, a public comment, testimony, and a report), with a deposit on Zenodo that mints a DOI.

title: Public Interest Data Science
section: What the book does not do
text:
What the book does not do
Honesty up front. This book is partial in several ways that matter.
It is US-centric. Most of the legal and administrative infrastructure discussed is American: FOIA and CORA, the Administrative Procedure Act, NIST, NSF, NYC Local Law 144. Where European, Latin American, and Global South counterparts exist (the Dutch SyRI case, IndiaStack, Ushahidi, the CARE Principles, Te Mana Raraunga), the book names them and points you to further reading, but it does not pretend to do them justice in three pages.
It is comfortable with records and less comfortable with refusal. The installed-base framework takes linkability, durable identifiers, and retention as load-bearing. Chapter 13 takes that comfort seriously as a limit, drawing on Zong and Matias, D’Ignazio and Klein, the CARE Principles, and Indigenous data sovereignty scholarship. Readers who want to start from refusal and arrive at records (rather than the other way around) should read Chapter 13 early and often.
It is thin on the labor inside data work. Gray and Suri’s Ghost Work is cited, and Chapter 11 tries to name invisible maintenance labor explicitly, but a book that seriously treated data-labor economics would look quite different. Consider this an invitation to the reader, or to the next edition.
It is thin on measurement theory. You will not find a full psychometric critique of the audit metrics in Chapter 8, and you will not find a deep philosophy-of-science treatment of what it means for a model to “work.” Those books exist and are cited.
It over-relies on the professional-lineage framing. Treating journalism, law, accounting, planning, and engineering as lineages the field can inherit from is a useful move, but every profession has its own pathologies, and the book does not do equal-time analysis of all of them. Read the criticisms. They are in the further-reading lists.
These limits are not bugs to be patched. They are framing choices that enable the book to cohere. Knowing where they bind is part of what you are learning, and 20  The Limits of the Framework turns the framework on itself to find out.

title: Public Interest Data Science
text:
How to contribute
This book lives in a git repository. Fork it, improve it, and open a pull request. Before you do, read claude.md, which codifies the voice, structure, and citation conventions. Typo fixes and small corrections can come in as pull requests directly. Rewrites of sections, new examples, or proposed new chapters should start as an issue so we can talk about them first.
Students in the companion course make one chapter-scale contribution each term: a new or rewritten section with narrative, a runnable tutorial, verified references, and curated resources. Students whose contributions shape the book are named in the acknowledgments. Some of the best chapters in future editions will be written by readers who encountered this one and saw what was missing.

title: Pressures and Values
text:
How the five chapters fit together
Every public decision that rests on data rests on something older than the data: identifiers someone agreed to keep, categories someone defined, archives someone paid to maintain, and offices someone empowered to act. When those arrangements hold, the public can check what its institutions know and contest what they decide. When they decay, the most careful analysis lands nowhere. This part of the book gives you the vocabulary for telling the two situations apart.
The vocabulary comes from Keegan (2026) and has three layers.
The first layer names three pressures that narrow the public’s capacity to observe and govern data-intensive systems. Enclosure asks who can observe: platforms close their APIs and agencies retire their datasets. Exemption asks who must answer: powerful firms and agencies operate beyond meaningful scrutiny, through formal carve-outs or through trade secrecy and technical control. Erosion asks what can be remembered: portals vanish, contracts lapse, and corpora develop holes nobody notices until a finding depends on them. The pressures reinforce each other. What is enclosed today is easier to erode tomorrow, and what has eroded cannot be scrutinized at all.
The second layer names three values that push back. Openness answers enclosure with the durable legibility of evidence, not merely access to files. Oversight answers exemption with routinized, testable scrutiny backed by an institution that can act on it. Ownership answers erosion with collective, accountable stewardship that outlasts any single grant or administration.
The third layer is the installed base: the socio-technical settlement where values become durable, or fail to. It has six elements. Records can be linked. Categories can be interpreted. Evidence has continuity across political cycles. Outsiders can practice safe scrutiny. Some office has the authority to act on what scrutiny finds. Affected people have a path to remedy. Most of this book’s diagnostic work comes down to asking which of the six is missing.
1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science opens with the problem the vocabulary is meant to solve: “the public interest” has been invoked to build expressways through neighborhoods and to enroll a billion people in a biometric identity system, by advocates and critics alike. Rather than define the phrase in the abstract, the chapter proposes treating it operationally, then has you retrieve your first public data from the Wikimedia pageviews API.
2  The Installed Base is the framework chapter. It situates the installed base among its intellectual predecessors (the politics of artifacts, the ecology and ethnography of infrastructure, classification and infrastructural inversion, the politics of data, sociotechnical imaginaries, and data infrastructure literacy), then lays out the pressures, values, six elements, and the five professional lineages the rest of the book borrows from. You build a minimum viable installed base for a small procurement log.
The three paired chapters each set one pressure against the value that answers it, with a bridge showing how the value works in practice. 3  Enclosure and Openness pairs enclosure with openness and builds a responsible scraper. 4  Exemption and Oversight pairs exemption with oversight, tracing a deployed screening tool through an evidence ledger and a remedy ledger. 5  Erosion and Ownership pairs erosion with ownership, including the sovereignty claims that complicate any easy account of who should own public-relevant data.
You can read these chapters in any order, and you will likely return to 2  The Installed Base as a reference. The lineages in Part II (6  Journalism to 10  Engineering), the adjacent conversations in Part III (11  Public Interest Technology and Data for Good to 13  Critical Data Studies, Data Justice, and Refusal), and the genres in Part IV (14  Op-Eds to 19  Archival Deposits) all use this part’s vocabulary as a diagnostic. 20  The Limits of the Framework asks where that diagnostic breaks.

title: Pressures and Values
text: Keegan, Brian C. 2026. “Public Interest Data Infrastructuring.” Under Review.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.1 What does “public interest” even mean
Open a newspaper any week and you will find a story about a data-driven system that has shaped a public decision in a way the public did not choose. A county’s child-welfare office screens families with an algorithm. A city’s benefits portal denies claims for reasons the claimants cannot discover. A federal agency’s climate database is quietly reorganized and three years of comparison data vanish. These are not exotic cases. They are ordinary governance in the 2020s.
This book is about the practice that takes those systems seriously as objects of public concern. Not as opportunities to build a better dashboard, though dashboards have their place. Not as abstract ethics problems, though ethics are unavoidable. As infrastructure: settled arrangements of data, code, authority, and labor that shape what the public can know and what it can demand. Public interest data science is the work of making that infrastructure observable, contestable, and, where necessary, reshaped.
The phrase “public interest” has an emancipatory history and an exclusionary one, and they are often the same history told from opposite sides of a highway.
Start with the highway. Robert Moses spent four decades building parks, bridges, and expressways in and around New York City, and he justified nearly all of it in the name of the public. Caro (1974) documents what that justification covered, including the Cross Bronx Expressway’s path through the East Tremont neighborhood, where the route displaced a working-class community that had asked for a modest alternative alignment. Jane Jacobs (1961) answered with a different public interest: the sidewalk, the mixed-use block, the residents already living where the planners drew their lines. Moses’s public was the motorist and the regional economy; Jacobs’s was the people on the block (Dory 2018). Both said “the public.”
Now cross an ocean and half a century. India’s Aadhaar program has issued a twelve-digit identity number, tied to fingerprints and iris scans, to more than a billion residents. Its advocates framed it as inclusion: an identity for people who had no documents, and an end to “leakage” in welfare programs where benefits went to duplicate or fictitious beneficiaries. Its critics, using the same vocabulary, documented people turned away from ration shops when fingerprint authentication failed, and warned that a single number linking every transaction would make a population legible to the state on terms the population never negotiated (Rao and Nair 2019). In 2017 the Supreme Court of India recognized privacy as a fundamental right in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India, and in 2018 the Court upheld Aadhaar for welfare delivery while striking down the provision that let private companies require it.  Both sides were arguing about who counts as the public, and what a data system owes the people it records.
That is why this book does not open with a tidy definition. Washington and Cheung (2024) go to history (public interest law, curb cuts, shared space) for what a public interest in technology could mean. Stapleton and colleagues (2022) ask the sharper question in their title: who has an interest in “public interest technology,” and who is left out when technologists working with local governments speak for impacted communities? “Public” is a word that asks: which public? Whose interests? Who was in the room?
The book does take a position, and it names the position explicitly. Following Keegan (2026), it treats the public interest as operational rather than abstract. The public interest is served when the six elements of what Chapter 2 calls the installed base are maintained. Records can be linked. Categories can be interpreted. Evidence persists across political cycles. Researchers and journalists can scrutinize systems without being sued or arrested. Someone has authority to act on what is learned. And the people affected have a path to remedy. When those six elements are in place, “public interest” is a working arrangement rather than a slogan. When they are missing, even the most benevolent data practice can produce what Eubanks (2018) calls automating inequality. Aadhaar is a useful test: it is superb at linkability and far weaker at remedy for the person whose fingerprint will not scan.
That is a particular theory, not the only one. Chapter 13 takes seriously the traditions (Indigenous data sovereignty, abolitionist critique, feminist refusal) that question whether “records” and “linkability” are the right starting places at all, and Chapter 20 returns to the framework’s limits. But you have to start somewhere.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.2 Relative to neighbors
Public interest data science overlaps with several fields you may already know. Data journalism investigates public questions computationally and publishes in the press; Chapter 6 treats journalism as a lineage. Public interest technology and data for good build tools and talent pipelines for government and civil society, usually on philanthropic money; Chapter 11 sorts them out. Digital government and civic tech build inside and around the state; Chapter 12 returns to them when procurement becomes the subject. Critical data studies and data justice theorize the politics of data and, at their sharpest, refuse it; Chapter 13 argues that your practice is stronger when it can absorb that critique. Public interest data science borrows from all of them.
crumbs: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.3 The arc of the book
The book has five parts. They move from diagnosis, to inheritance, to argument with neighbors, to practice, and finally to the framework’s own limits.
Part I, Pressures and Values (this chapter through Chapter 5), gives you the vocabulary. Chapter 2 introduces three pressures that narrow public knowledge (enclosure, exemption, erosion), three values that push back (openness, oversight, ownership), and the six elements of the installed base, and it places that framework among its intellectual predecessors. The three chapters after it each pair one pressure with the value that answers it.
Part II, Lineages (Chapter 6 to Chapter 10), asks what data science can inherit from five professions that already built public interest traditions: journalism, law, accounting and auditing, planning, and engineering. Each solved a version of your problem, and each carries an exclusionary past you inherit along with the method.
Part III, Adjacent Conversations (Chapter 11 to Chapter 13), maps the neighbors described above and asks what each builds and what it leaves unbuilt.
Part IV, Genres (Chapter 14 to Chapter 19), turns analysis into public contribution: op-eds, reports, research proposals, testimony, public comments, and archival deposits. Each chapter ends with an artifact you have actually produced, paired with code someone else can run.
Part V, Closing (Chapter 20), turns the framework on itself and asks where it fails.
You do not have to read the chapters in order. Each one names the concepts it relies on and links to the chapter that develops them, whether that chapter comes earlier or later. If you need to testify next month, start at Chapter 17 and follow its links back to Chapter 7 and Chapter 4. If you are auditing a model, start at Chapter 8. Courses that use the book, including the one it was written alongside, assign chapters out of sequence. The one chapter worth reading early is Chapter 2, because nearly every other chapter uses its vocabulary as a diagnostic.

1.3.1 Each lineage has a level
Evidence matters only if it reaches a body with the authority to act on it, and different public bodies listen through different channels. The lineages and genres therefore each have a natural level of government, and the book’s worked examples follow it.

So a journalism chapter works with city records in Boulder and Denver, and the op-ed chapter pitches a city outlet. The planning chapter works with Boulder County’s land use records, and the public comment goes to a county board. The law chapter treats Colorado statutes as rule makers, and the testimony goes to a committee of the Colorado General Assembly. The accounting and engineering chapters audit federal systems, and the report goes to a named federal body. The anchor cases (Moses in New York, Aadhaar in India) and the non-US counter-cases may sit at any level, because their job is to test whether the framework travels. Chapter 2 says more about why each lineage lands where it does.
The book is also a public repository, and it is wrong in places you will find before the author does. Pull requests are welcome.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.4 A first request
Enough about the book. Do something with it. The rest of this chapter is a twenty-minute tour of the toolkit, built around a first public data retrieval. The Environment setup sidebar below lists what you need.






NoteEnvironment setup



You need Python 3.11 or newer, git, and a working command line. On macOS and Linux, python3 --version and git --version should return something reasonable. On Windows, WSL2 works well, as does the official Python installer with the “Add Python to PATH” box ticked. You will also want pip install pandas requests matplotlib jupyter before continuing, and a GitHub account if you do not have one already.


You will retrieve pageview data for the Wikipedia article “Public interest” in three language editions and see how the concept’s visibility varies across linguistic publics. The example is small, but it installs habits that recur: fetching from a real public API, handling the response carefully, moving it into a pandas DataFrame, plotting it, and asking what the data can and cannot tell you.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.5 The Wikimedia pageviews API
Wikimedia Foundation operates a pageviews API that returns view counts for any article on any of their projects, back to 2015. The endpoints are documented at wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1. The relevant endpoint takes the form:
GET /metrics/pageviews/per-article/{project}/{access}/{agent}/{article}/{granularity}/{start}/{end}
You plug in the project (e.g., en.wikipedia), access method (all-access is fine), agent type (user filters out bots and spiders, which you want), article title, and a start and end date in YYYYMMDD or YYYYMMDDHH format.
Here is a first retrieval:
import requests

HEADERS = {
    "User-Agent": "PublicInterestDataScience/0.1 (your-email@example.edu)",
    "Accept": "application/json",
}

url = (
    "https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/"
    "en.wikipedia/all-access/user/Public_interest/monthly/"
    "2020010100/2024123100"
)

response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
response.raise_for_status()
data = response.json()
print(data["items"][:2])
# => [{'project': 'en.wikipedia', 'article': 'Public_interest',
#      'granularity': 'monthly', 'timestamp': '2020010100',
#      'access': 'all-access', 'agent': 'user', 'views': 8442}, ...]
You did three things there that you will keep doing: you sent a User-Agent header naming yourself, called raise_for_status() to turn HTTP errors into exceptions, and set a timeout so a hung server does not hang your script. Chapter 3 turns these habits into a full “responsible scraper” function. For now, notice that requests.get() does not hand you the response body directly. It hands you a Response object, and .json() is one of several methods you can call on it.






TipThe Missing Manual



Most tutorials teach you requests.get(url).json() as a single chained call. That works until it does not. The Response object carries the status code, headers, cookies, and error context separately from the body. When a request fails (and it will), you need the status code and the headers to understand why; calling .json() on a 403 will give you an exception that hides the 403. Write your code so the Response survives long enough to inspect. You will thank yourself the first time an API silently starts returning an HTML error page in place of JSON.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.6 Into pandas
A single JSON response is interesting. Three parallel time series for three language editions are more so. Collect “Public interest” pageviews for English, Spanish, and Hindi Wikipedia and plot them side by side.
import pandas as pd

def fetch_pageviews(project, article, start="2020010100", end="2024123100"):
    url = (
        f"https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/metrics/pageviews/per-article/"
        f"{project}/all-access/user/{article}/monthly/{start}/{end}"
    )
    response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=30)
    response.raise_for_status()
    items = response.json()["items"]
    df = pd.DataFrame(items)
    df["timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(df["timestamp"], format="%Y%m%d%H")
    return df[["timestamp", "project", "views"]]

en = fetch_pageviews("en.wikipedia", "Public_interest")
es = fetch_pageviews("es.wikipedia", "Interés_público")
hi = fetch_pageviews("hi.wikipedia", "लोक_हित")

combined = pd.concat([en, es, hi], ignore_index=True)
combined.groupby("project")["views"].describe()
# => project-level descriptive stats across 60 months
Already the choices are political. The English article is titled “Public interest.” The Spanish equivalent is “Interés público.” The Hindi article is “लोक हित,” which translates roughly as “people’s good” rather than “interest.” These are not translations in the sense a machine would call translations; they are conceptually distinct articles that Wikipedia’s interlanguage links happen to join. The fact that all three exist tells you something. The fact that their pageview trajectories differ tells you something else.
Plot them:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
for project, group in combined.groupby("project"):
    ax.plot(group["timestamp"], group["views"], label=project)
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_ylabel("Views")
ax.set_title("Wikipedia pageviews: 'Public interest' across three editions")
ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("ch01_pageviews.png", dpi=120)
If your plot looks reasonable, you have just run an end-to-end public interest data pipeline. Not a large one, but a real one: it fetches from a public API, handles errors, reshapes JSON into a DataFrame, and produces a figure legible in a campus paper or a policy brief.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.7 Reading the plot
Three things to notice, because they recur.
First, the series do not share a calendar. Look for months where the English series spikes and the Spanish or Hindi series does not, and ask what was in the news in each place that month. A single global “public interest” is a fiction; there are many publics, and their interests peak at different times.
Second, all three series are small relative to any major news article. “Public interest” is a reference concept, not a subject of mass curiosity. The audience for public interest work is small but reachable, if you know where it is.
Third, the data will drift. Wikipedia articles get renamed, redirected, merged. The endpoint you called today may return a different trajectory next year because the article itself has changed. Chapter 5 takes up the problem of what can be remembered; this exercise is your first tiny encounter with it.






NoteIn the Public Interest



Three line plots of Wikipedia pageviews look like a trifle. Notice what they required. A public API, documented and open. Endpoints that return consistent, structured data. A retention policy that preserves history for at least a decade. A User-Agent expectation that asks you to identify yourself rather than hiding. Wikipedia built these as deliberate commitments to openness (Chapter 3). If you were trying to do the same exercise against a commercial platform in 2026, you would find most of those commitments have been withdrawn. The pressure of enclosure (Chapter 3) makes the simple thing you just did unusually precious. Part of this book’s work is to help you notice when the simple thing is rare.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.8 Exercises
Exercise 1.1 (Guided). Install Python 3.11+, git, and the packages listed in the environment setup callout. Create a public GitHub repository for your work with this book and clone it. Create a branch named yourname/intro. Add a file introductions/yourname.md with three sentences: who you are, a public you belong to, and a level of government whose decisions you have felt directly. Commit with the message intro: yourname, push, and open a pull request against your own main branch. The content matters less than the mechanism. Branch, commit, and pull request are a good default for every exercise in this book, and the same mechanism is how you would propose a correction to the book itself.
Exercise 1.2 (Guided, real public data). Adapt the pageviews script to retrieve monthly views for three Wikipedia articles you care about, across three language editions each. Produce one plot comparing them. Write 150 words interpreting it. Save the plot and writeup to exercises/ch01_pageviews/. Record one choice (article, language, or date range) you had to make, and why.
Exercise 1.3 (Reflective). Write a 300-word “data obituary” for an API, dataset, or data portal that has been withdrawn, paywalled, or substantially restricted. Reddit’s Pushshift is a classic candidate. Name the source, say what it was useful for, describe what happened to it, and identify who has been worse off since. Cite two sources.
Exercise 1.4 (Analytic). Find a recent public document from a city, county, state, or federal body in which someone invokes “the public interest” (a council resolution, a court filing, an agency press release, a records denial). Write 300 words answering: which public does the document mean, who is left out, and what would have to be on the record for an outsider to check the claim? Compare your answer with the Moses or Aadhaar case.
Exercise 1.5 (Open-ended). What is a public interest data question you want to answer with the tools in this book? Write two to three paragraphs: the question, who would benefit, what data would be needed, which level of government could act on the answer, and what obstacles you already see. Save it as exercises/ch01_project_sketch.md. Revisit it after each part of the book. By the time you reach the genres in Part IV, it should be specific enough to become a submittable artifact: an op-ed, a report section, testimony, or a public comment, depending on which level of government can act on the answer.

title: 1  Introduction to Public Interest Data Science
text:
1.9 Looking ahead
Chapter 2 gives you the full vocabulary in one sitting: the three pressures of enclosure, exemption, and erosion; the three values of openness, oversight, and ownership; the six elements of the installed base; and the five lineages the rest of the book borrows from. It also places the installed base among its intellectual predecessors, from the politics of artifacts to data infrastructure literacy, and explains why each lineage has a natural level of government. Then you will build a minimum viable installed base for a small civic dataset, because the vocabulary is only useful if you can see it in a file.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.1 Predecessors and parallels
Chapter 1 argued that “the public interest” is contested and promised a working definition instead of a tidy one. This chapter delivers it. The definition rests on one idea: the installed base, the inherited arrangement of records, categories, archives, protections, offices, and appeals that determines whether anyone can check what a data-intensive system did and do something about it. Around that idea sit three pressures that narrow public knowledge, three values that push back, and five professional lineages that have built installed bases before.
The idea did not come from nowhere. Science and technology studies, information studies, and critical data studies spent four decades arguing that technical systems carry politics, that infrastructure is relational and mostly invisible, and that data are made rather than found. The chapter begins with that inheritance, because knowing what each predecessor contributes, and where the installed base departs from it, keeps the framework honest. It ends by building a small installed base in code. Treat the chapter as a map you will keep unfolding; most of its ideas get a chapter of their own later.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.1.1 The politics of artifacts
Langdon Winner (1980) asked whether artifacts have politics and answered yes, in two senses. Some technologies are designed, deliberately or not, to settle a political question: his best-known example is the low overpasses on Robert Moses’s Long Island parkways, which Winner, following Caro (1974), read as a way to keep buses, and the poorer and Black New Yorkers who rode them, off the road to the beaches. Other technologies are “inherently political” because they require, or are strongly compatible with, particular arrangements of power; his starkest example is the atom bomb, whose existence demands a centralized, hierarchical chain of command. The bridge story has been contested on the evidence (Joerges 1999), which is itself a lesson about how much weight a single anecdote can carry.
Winner gives you permission to treat a schema, an API, or a retention schedule as a political object. The installed base differs in where it looks. Winner’s politics are mostly fixed at design; the installed base’s politics are made and unmade in maintenance, by whoever keeps assigning identifiers, documenting categories, and paying for the archive.


2.1.2 The ecology and ethnography of infrastructure
Star and Ruhleder (1996) studied the Worm Community System, a networked collaboration tool for biologists, and concluded that the useful question is not what an infrastructure is but when it is one. Infrastructure is relational: the same system is invisible plumbing to one person and an obstacle to another. They listed its properties, including that it is embedded in other structures, learned as part of membership in a community, linked to conventions of practice, built on an installed base, and visible upon breakdown. (An earlier conference version is Star and Ruhleder (1994).) Star (1999) then urged researchers to study such “boring things” and offered methods for reading them, such as surfacing the invisible work that keeps them running.
This is the book’s most direct ancestor, and the term is theirs. The difference is purpose. Star and Ruhleder described how infrastructure works for a community of practice. Keegan (2026) asks a normative question of the same object: does the installed base let an outsider, especially an affected one, hold a system to account?


2.1.3 Classification and infrastructural inversion
Bowker and Star’s Sorting Things Out (2000), first published in 1999, examined classification systems such as the International Classification of Diseases and the racial categories of apartheid South Africa. Every classification makes some things visible and others invisible, and the consequences fall on the people sorted. Their method is infrastructural inversion: deliberately reversing figure and ground so that the backstage work of a system (the forms, standards, and judgment calls) becomes the object of study instead of the background to it.
Inversion is the method this book uses most, though it rarely says so. When you ask who assigned a dataset’s identifiers or why a column has the categories it has, you are inverting. What the installed base adds is a checklist for after the inversion. Inversion shows you what is there; the six elements tell you what is missing for accountability.


2.1.4 The politics of data
Paul Edwards’s A Vast Machine (2010) shows that global climate knowledge depends on a century of observing stations, reporting standards, and models, and that moving data across institutional boundaries carries real costs he calls data friction. Climate scientists constantly invert their own infrastructure, revisiting how old readings were taken and adjusting them, and critics of climate science have repeatedly cast such revisions as manipulation. The politics of data includes the politics of correction. boyd and Crawford (2012) made a parallel argument about platform data: claims to objectivity are misleading, and limited access to big data creates new divides between those who can study it and those who cannot, an early description of what this book calls enclosure.
Both works argue that data are made, by people and institutions with interests. The installed base accepts that and asks a narrower question: given that data are made, what must be in place for the making to be inspected and contested?


2.1.5 Sociotechnical imaginaries
Jasanoff and Kim (2009) compared nuclear power in the United States, framed as a dangerous force needing containment and regulation, with South Korea, framed as an engine of national development. They called such visions sociotechnical imaginaries, and their later volume (Jasanoff and Kim 2015) broadened the idea beyond nations to “collectively held, institutionally stabilized, and publicly performed visions of desirable futures” that science and technology are meant to help deliver. “Smart cities,” “data-driven government,” and “open by default” are imaginaries in this sense.
Imaginaries explain why infrastructures get funded. The installed base describes what remains when the vision fades and the grant ends. Be honest about one thing: the three values in this chapter are an imaginary too, and Chapter 20 treats them that way.


2.1.6 Data infrastructure literacy
Gray, Gerlitz, and Bounegru (2018) argue that data literacy should cover not only reading and working with datasets but also “the ability to account for, intervene around and participate in the wider socio-technical infrastructures through which data is created, stored and analysed.” They draw examples from data journalism and data activism. This is close to the book’s own pedagogical aim. The difference is that literacy is a capacity of people, while the installed base is a property of arrangements. You need both: literate people facing an installed base with no authority or remedy can describe the problem precisely and still change nothing.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.2 Three pressures
Keegan (2026) names three mutually reinforcing forces. Each answers a question.
Enclosure asks who can observe. It is the privatization or withdrawal of data that once held public or research value. Facebook restricted its APIs after Cambridge Analytica; Twitter revoked research access after its 2022 acquisition; Reddit ended Pushshift’s access and priced its API beyond most researchers. Freelon (2018) calls the result a “post-API age.” Governments enclose too, when they retire datasets on policing, health, or the environment. Chapter 3 develops the pressure.
Exemption asks who must answer. It is the capacity of powerful firms and agencies to operate beyond meaningful scrutiny. Keegan distinguishes legal exemption (formal carve-outs, thin duties, jurisdictional gaps) from practical exemption (trade secrecy, restrictive terms of service, technical controls that make scrutiny infeasible). The systems with the greatest public consequences face the weakest oversight (Pasquale 2016). Chapter 4 develops it, and Chapter 8 meets its most polished form, audit-washing.
Erosion asks what can be remembered. It is the decay of the institutions and infrastructures that make long-term observation possible: portals that vanish, contracts that lapse, corpora with silent holes (Gaffney and Matias 2018; Plantin et al. 2016). Erosion is rarely dramatic, which is what makes it effective. Chapter 5 develops it.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.3 Three values
Openness counters enclosure. It is the durable legibility of evidentiary traces: not only access to files, but provenance, documentation, and reproducible workflows that let more than experts evaluate how data were made (Chapter 3).
Oversight counters exemption. It is routinized, testable scrutiny: audits, documentation standards, impact assessments, and institutions with authority to act on what they find. Chapter 4 treats oversight as remedy; Chapter 8 and Chapter 10 treat it as independent verification.
Ownership counters erosion. It does not mean private property. It means collective, accountable governance over the preservation, access, and use of public-relevant data, with stewardship obligations that outlast any one grant or administration. Chapter 5 develops it, including the sovereignty claims that complicate it.
Values stated in a mission statement are cheap. They become durable only when they are built into something.

title: 2  The Installed Base
section: 2.4 The installed base and its six elements
text:
2.4 The installed base and its six elements
New infrastructure never lands on a blank site. It inherits prior wiring, formats, routines, and labor, the way a neighborhood inherits its streets. Karasti and Blomberg (2018) call the ongoing work of keeping infrastructure aligned with what the installed base will tolerate infrastructuring, and Aanestad and colleagues (2017) show national health-IT programs failing, repeatedly, by ignoring it. Keegan (2026) extends the idea: for public interest work, the installed base is the socio-technical settlement that makes accountability possible. It has six elements.
Linkability. Records carry stable identifiers that let them be referenced and joined across time and systems. Someone must have the duty to assign references and carry them through reorganizations.
Interpretability. Categories, units, and transformations are documented well enough for a qualified outsider, including an affected party, to reason about them. Classification is never neutral (Bowker and Star 2000); interpretability lets you see the classification and argue with it.
Continuity. Evidence persists across political cycles, vendor changes, and budget gaps. It is a resourcing commitment more than a technical feature: retention schedules, mirrors, migration plans, and paid maintainers.
Safe scrutiny. Researchers, journalists, auditors, and communities can examine the system without being sued, arrested, or retaliated against. Tiered access belongs here: governed visibility that protects people without becoming an excuse for exemption.
Authority. A named office has the responsibility and power to act on what scrutiny reveals. An audit that lands on no one’s desk is a training exercise.
Remedy. The people affected have accessible, protected, consequential paths to contest decisions and correct the record. Remedy often has no software layer at all; it lives in appeals, ombuds offices, and organizing.
The order matters: you cannot offer remedy over records nobody can link. The elements also map onto the values. Openness operationalizes linkability, interpretability, and much of continuity. Oversight operationalizes safe scrutiny and authority. Ownership operationalizes remedy and the stewardship that keeps continuity from collapsing into somebody’s weekend hobby.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.5 Five lineages
Data science did not invent the problem of making expertise answer to the public. Keegan (2026) identifies five professions that built public interest traditions by infrastructuring: turning a value into records, routines, and institutions.
Journalism maintains the evidentiary surface of public life through archives, verification, and publication (Chapter 6). Law translates values into enforceable procedures: rights to access, duties to disclose, standards of review, and remedies (Chapter 7). Accounting built a public interest mandate around independence and verification after audits failed the public (Baker 2005) (Chapter 8). Planning learned, through advocacy planning (Davidoff 1965) and the backlash against figures like Moses, that technical choices allocate burdens across space and time, and that affected people belong in the room (Chapter 9). Engineering made safety, testing, and incident learning into codes (Petroski 1992) (Chapter 10).
Every lineage also has an exclusionary past. Borrowing a method means borrowing its blind spots, and each lineage chapter asks you to name them.

title: 2  The Installed Base
section: 2.6 The natural level of each lineage
text:
2.6 The natural level of each lineage
The authority element implies that evidence matters only if it reaches a body that can act on it. Each lineage, and the genre that carries its work to the public, has a natural level of government where that body sits.

City: journalism and op-eds. City records are abundant and scattered, local news has thinned, and an op-ed in a local outlet can be read by every council member (Chapter 6, Chapter 14).
County: planning and public comments. Counties zone unincorporated land, adopt comprehensive plans, and keep land use dockets; Boulder County’s Planning Commission and Board of County Commissioners take public comment, and the county publishes what it releases under open records requests (Chapter 9, Chapter 18).
State: law and testimony. The state writes the rules: open-records statutes such as the Colorado Open Records Act (Colorado General Assembly 1968) and AI legislation such as Colorado’s AI Act, passed in 2024 as SB 24-205 and repealed and reenacted in 2026 as SB 26-189 (Colorado General Assembly 2024, 2026). Committees of the Colorado General Assembly hear testimony during the session, which runs from January into May (Chapter 7, Chapter 17).
Nation: accounting, engineering, and reports. Federal agencies deploy automated decision systems, publish AI use-case inventories, and answer to the GAO, inspectors general, congressional committees, and standards bodies like NIST (Chapter 8, Chapter 10, Chapter 15).

These are defaults, not walls. Anchor cases and non-US counter-cases sit at whatever level they happened at, real problems cross levels, and the stack itself is a US federal arrangement that other countries organize differently.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.7 Diagnosing a missing element
The framework earns its keep diagnostically. Take the Allegheny Family Screening Tool, which Chapter 4 treats in detail. Linkability is good: each hotline call is joined to administrative records. Interpretability is partial: features are documented, weights are harder to reason about (Vaithianathan et al. 2019). Continuity is maintained by named teams. The tail is weak. Safe scrutiny depends on the county’s willingness to cooperate with outside researchers. Authority sits with call screeners who can override the score but feel pressure not to. Remedy for a family flagged and investigated is almost nonexistent; you cannot unring a caseworker visit. The framework does not tell you what to do. It tells you where to look, so that an intervention lands somewhere that will hold it.






NoteIn the Public Interest



The installed base is where openness, oversight, and ownership stop being rhetorical. A city portal that earns a five-star “open data” rating can still fail openness in the sense this book uses, if its URLs break at every vendor rebid and nobody preserves the raw extracts, because continuity is part of legibility. Oversight fails when findings have no authority to land on, however good the audit. Ownership fails when the steward is a volunteer with no successor. When you see the three values named abstractly elsewhere, translate back to the six elements. That translation is the discipline this chapter teaches, and the note on provenance and gaps that accompanies each artifact in Part IV is the place to perform it.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.8 A minimum viable installed base
Enough vocabulary. You cannot talk seriously about the six elements without building a version of them at least once. The dataset is a procurement log for a fictional small city: 500 contract awards with two deliberate failures. Some rows are missing identifiers, and some amounts went through an undocumented currency conversion. Generate it yourself so the tutorial runs anywhere:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(4871)
n = 500
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "record_id": [f"SC-{i:05d}" for i in range(n)],
    "vendor": rng.choice(["Acme Paving", "Front Range IT", "Rhein GmbH",
                          "Liffey Consulting", "Flatirons Print"], n),
    "amount": rng.lognormal(10, 1, n).round(2),
    "award_date": pd.date_range("2021-01-01", periods=n, freq="3D"),
    "award_type": rng.choice(["bid", "sole_source", "emergency"], n),
    "contact_email": [f"vendor{i}@example.com" for i in range(n)],
    "contract_reference": [f"C-{2021 + i // 125}-{i:04d}" for i in range(n)],
})
df.loc[rng.choice(n, 28, replace=False), "record_id"] = None
df["record_id"].isna().sum()
# => 28

2.8.1 Linkability: persistent identifiers
Two reasonable ways to fill the 28 gaps: a random UUID, or a hash of the record’s own content. A UUID is opaque and survives corrections; a content hash detects silent changes but shifts the moment anyone fixes a typo. For civic records, where correction is expected, use both. The UUID is the canonical identifier; the content hash is a side channel you can log over time as a change history.
import hashlib
import uuid

def content_hash(row):
    payload = f"{row['vendor']}|{row['amount']}|{row['award_date']}|{row['award_type']}"
    return hashlib.sha256(payload.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

missing = df["record_id"].isna()
df.loc[missing, "record_id"] = [str(uuid.uuid4()) for _ in range(missing.sum())]
df["content_hash"] = df.apply(content_hash, axis=1)
df["record_id"].is_unique
# => True






TipThe Missing Manual



UUIDs are the easy part. Every language ships a generator. The hard part is durable reference, and durable reference is social work. Somebody has to maintain the resolver (the service that turns an identifier into a record), hold the naming authority (who may mint identifiers), and make the migration commitment (when systems change, identifiers move with them). DOIs work because Crossref and DataCite exist as institutions, not because the string 10.1234/... is clever. Your procurement log’s identifiers will work if, and only if, some office commits to carrying them across the next three vendor contracts. If nobody has signed up, you have a UUID, not an identifier.




2.8.2 Interpretability: a provenance document
In the real version of this log, the rows from Rhein GmbH and Liffey Consulting arrived in euros and were converted to dollars by someone who never wrote it down. An auditor who assumes the source was always in dollars will misreport. The fix is not code. It is a provenance document committed next to the data, readable by people and machines.
# data/provenance.yaml
dataset: smallcity_procurement
version: "2.0"
upstream_source:
  name: Small City Department of Finance, ERP export
  accessed: 2026-03-12
transformations:
  - step: 01_extract
    description: CSV export from the accounts-payable module.
  - step: 02_currency_normalize
    description: >
      Rows for vendors in DE and IE carried EUR amounts. Converted to USD
      using the ECB monthly reference rate for the award_date month.
    rate_source: https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/policy_and_exchange_rates/
  - step: 03_identifier_assignment
    description: UUID minted for 28 rows with missing record_id; content_hash added.
known_issues:
  - Monthly average rates; daily rates not preserved.


2.8.3 Continuity: a retention policy
Continuity without a retention policy is an act of faith. Write it down in a form that survives its author leaving the job.
# data/retention.yaml
schedule:
  raw_extracts:      {retain_for: 10_years,   storage: city_records_archive}
  published_versions: {retain_for: indefinite, storage: zenodo_plus_ia_mirror}
  derivation_scripts: {retain_for: indefinite, storage: city_git}
  access_logs:       {retain_for: 2_years,    purpose: audit_restricted_queries}
responsible_office: Department of Finance, Data Stewardship Lead
review_cadence: annual


2.8.4 Safe scrutiny and authority: tiered access
Vendor names and contract totals are public records almost everywhere. Contact details for sole proprietors often should not be. SQLite views express the tiers: the table holds the full record and each view is a lens on it.
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect("smallcity_procurement.db")
df.to_sql("procurement", con, if_exists="replace", index=False)
con.executescript("""
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS v_public;
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS v_authenticated;
CREATE VIEW v_public AS
  SELECT record_id, vendor, amount, award_date, award_type FROM procurement;
CREATE VIEW v_authenticated AS
  SELECT record_id, vendor, amount, award_date, award_type,
         contact_email, contract_reference FROM procurement;
""")
con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM v_public").fetchone()
# => (500,)
In production you would enforce tiers with row-level security or an API gateway. Here the view definitions make the commitments legible: anyone reading the schema can see what each tier may see, which is how safe scrutiny avoids collapsing into “publish everything” or “publish nothing.”


2.8.5 Remedy: an escalation log
Access without escalation is a suggestion box nobody empties. The last file says who is notified when something happens, and how fast they must respond. Keep it boring.
# data/escalation.yaml
routes:
  - trigger: correction request received
    notify: [records_officer, affected_department]
    sla: 10_business_days
    remedy: issue corrected row, log in change_history
  - trigger: removal request (privacy or safety)
    notify: [city_attorney, records_officer]
    sla: 5_business_days
    remedy: redaction, tombstone record retained
  - trigger: restricted view accessed
    notify: [records_officer, audit_log]

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.9 What this demonstrates
In about a hundred lines you built a minimum viable installed base: identifiers for linkability, a provenance file for interpretability, a retention policy for continuity, tiered views for safe scrutiny, and an escalation log naming the offices that hold authority and owe remedy. It is not a dashboard, a model, or an “AI governance” framework. It is the plumbing under all of them, and Keegan (2026) calls attending to it the infrastructuring move: treating what looks like a platform problem as an installed-base problem. The tutorial was also an inversion in Bowker and Star’s sense, run in reverse: instead of excavating someone else’s backstage, you wrote your own down.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.10 Exercises
Exercise 2.1 (Guided). Run the tutorial end to end and save the result as exercises/ch02_procurement_v2.csv. In 150 words, explain why the tutorial makes the UUID, not the content hash, the canonical record_id, and describe one situation where you would choose the opposite. Then write one query against the database and say which tier may run it.
Exercise 2.2 (Guided). Extend provenance.yaml with one transformation step of your own (vendor-name normalization, deduplication) and add a contact field naming a responsible office. Then write retention.yaml for a city or organization you know, citing one real records-retention schedule to justify at least one retention period.
Exercise 2.3 (Diagnostic, real public data). Pick one dataset from the State of Colorado’s portal at data.colorado.gov, which runs on Socrata and exposes metadata at /api/views/<dataset-id>.json. Fetch the metadata with requests and record the license, the last-updated timestamp, the publishing department, and how many columns have descriptions. Score the dataset on all six elements (0 to 2 each), with one sentence of evidence per score. Which element would you fix first, and which office has the authority to fix it? 500 words plus your script.
Exercise 2.4 (Infrastructural inversion, real public data). Invert New York City’s 311 Service Requests dataset (Socrata ID erm2-nwe9). Fetch https://data.cityofnewyork.us/api/views/erm2-nwe9.json and read the description and column list as evidence about the system that produces the rows, not the rows themselves. In October 2026 the dataset was titled “311 Service Requests from 2020 to Present,” its description pointed to a separate dataset for 2010 to 2019, and it described itself as covering “only service requests that can be directed to specific agencies.” Answer four questions in 600 words: Who generates a row (see open_data_channel_type), and who never does? Who maintains the complaint_type and descriptor vocabularies, and what would you need to see their history? What does the split at 2020 do to linkability and continuity? Which office could you ask about any of this? Substitute a 311 dataset from your own city if it has one.
Exercise 2.5 (Open). Design an escalation pathway and a threat model for a small civic dataset of your choosing (school board minutes, a housing-permit feed, a campus crime log). Name at least three triggers, the offices notified, and a service-level agreement for each, plus three adversaries (not all malicious; an underfunded vendor counts) and one failure mode for each. 800 to 1,200 words. You will return to this pattern when you build a remedy ledger in Chapter 4.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.11 Looking ahead
The three paired chapters that follow take one pressure and its value at a time: enclosure and openness in Chapter 3, exemption and oversight in Chapter 4, erosion and ownership in Chapter 5. If you would rather start with a profession, the lineages begin at Chapter 6; if you want to know how this framework relates to public interest technology and civic tech, turn to Chapter 11. Whichever you choose, carry the six elements with you.

title: 2  The Installed Base
text:
2.12 Further Reading and Resources

Susan Leigh Star and Karen Ruhleder (1996), “Steps toward an ecology of infrastructure,” Information Systems Research 7(1): 111–134 (Star and Ruhleder 1996). Where “installed base” comes from.
Susan Leigh Star (1999), “The ethnography of infrastructure,” American Behavioral Scientist 43(3): 377–391 (STAR 1999). A short methods guide to studying boring things.
Geoffrey C. Bowker and Susan Leigh Star, Sorting Things Out (Bowker and Star 2000). Classification and infrastructural inversion.

Jonathan Gray, Carolin Gerlitz, and Liliana Bounegru (2018), “Data infrastructure literacy,” Big Data & Society 5(2) (Gray et al. 2018). Open access.
Helena Karasti and Jeanette Blomberg (2018), “Studying infrastructuring ethnographically,” Computer Supported Cooperative Work 27: 233–265 (Karasti and Blomberg 2018). Infrastructuring as alignment work.
Socrata Open Data API documentation: https://dev.socrata.com/. The API behind the portals in Exercises 2.3 and 2.4.







Aanestad, Margunn, Miria Grisot, Ole Hanseth, and Polyxeni Vassilakopoulou. 2017. “Information Infrastructures and the Challenge of the Installed Base.” Information Infrastructures Within European Health Care, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-51020-0_3.


Baker, C. Richard. 2005. “What Is the Meaning of ‘the Public Interest’? Examining the Ideology of the American Public Accounting Profession.” Accounting, Auditing & Accountability Journal 18 (5): 690–703. https://doi.org/10.1108/09513570510620510.


Bowker, Geoffrey C., and Susan Leigh Star. 2000. Sorting Things Out: Classification and Its Consequences. MIT Press. https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262522953/sorting-things-out/.
