title: 7  Law
text:
7.1 Public interest lawyering as a profession
A list of things a government has not told you cannot make anyone answer. A statute can. With a public-records law behind you, you write a different kind of letter: one that cites a section of code, starts a statutory clock, and preserves the right to go to court. The letter is still a request. What makes it work is the legal infrastructure behind it.
Law is a lineage worth borrowing from because few professions have thought harder about pursuing the public interest under adversarial conditions. Keegan (2026) describes public interest law as the lineage that “translates values into enforceable procedures”: rights to access, duties to disclose, standards of review, and remedies. In the United States most of those procedures that touch local data are written by states. A state legislature decides what a city or county must disclose, how fast, at what price, and what a requester may do when refused; what budget a county must adopt and file; and, increasingly, what duties attach to automated decision systems.
The rule maker in this chapter is the Colorado General Assembly. You will read the Colorado Open Records Act (CORA) as a statute, watch the legislature decline to weaken it, and read the Colorado AI Act as state accountability law in the making. You will see the statute at work in one county’s practice: the Public Records Archive in Boulder County’s Open Records Center, where the county posts requests others filed and it has already answered. You will leave with a SQLite tracker, a critical eye for request letters, and a notebook that turns a county PDF produced under state budget law into a table you can check.
Albiston and Nielsen (2017) show that public interest lawyering is not a specialty like tax or real estate but a stance toward practice: representing interests the market will not pay to represent, often for clients whose stake in an outcome is structural rather than individual. Cause lawyering, the term Sarat and Scheingold (1998) put at the center of the field’s self-understanding, treats a case as an instrument for changing a rule rather than a dispute between two parties.
Albiston and Nielsen find a two-tier structure: a few well-funded organizations working on appellate strategy and legislative advocacy, and a much larger tier of legal aid societies and clinics absorbing front-line demand. Records requests are second-tier work, and this chapter’s tools aim there; legislative testimony (Chapter 17) is how front-line evidence reaches the first tier’s arena.

title: 7  Law
text:
7.2 CORA as a statute
The federal Freedom of Information Act, with its nine exemptions (US Congress 1966), does not reach states, cities, or counties. Every state has its own statute, and Colorado’s is CORA, C.R.S. § 24-72-201 et seq. (Colorado General Assembly 1968). Read it as machinery with four parts.

The clock. Records are due within a “reasonable time,” presumed to be three working days, extendable by up to seven more if the custodian finds extenuating circumstances in writing within the first three (Colorado Freedom of Information Coalition 2024).
The exemptions. Section 24-72-204 sorts withholding into tiers. Inspection may be refused where it would be contrary to a state or federal statute or a court rule or order. The custodian may deny certain records, among them law enforcement investigatory files and the details of bona fide research projects at state institutions, if disclosure would be “contrary to the public interest.” The custodian shall deny others, among them personnel files, medical data on individuals, letters of reference, trade secrets and confidential commercial data, and records under the deliberative process privilege, for which the custodian owes the requester a sworn statement describing each document withheld.
The fees. The first hour of research and retrieval is free. After that the hourly fee is capped, with the cap adjusted every five years for Denver-area inflation; since July 1, 2024 it has been $41.37 (Roberts 2024). A custodian may charge only under a written policy published in advance. Fee waivers are discretionary, not a right. 
The remedies. There is no administrative appeal. A requester who is denied gives the custodian at least fourteen days’ written notice and then applies to the district court for an order to show cause. Unless the court finds the denial proper, it must award costs and reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing applicant (Colorado Freedom of Information Coalition 2024). In the other direction, a custodian who believes disclosure of an otherwise public record would do “substantial injury to the public interest” may ask the court for permission to withhold it.

Criminal justice records follow a separate statute, the Colorado Criminal Justice Records Act (CCJRA), whose “public interest” balancing test the custodian applies and must articulate; Boulder County routes Sheriff’s Office requests through a separate page. That shapes how you write. A request for “all emails from the Sheriff mentioning license plate readers” invites the custodian to treat everything as a criminal justice record. A request for “administrative records concerning the procurement and contracting of automated license plate reader technology, including contracts, invoices, and vendor correspondence” names administrative categories and makes that classification harder to justify.
The statute is not finished. In 2025 the General Assembly passed SB 25-077, lengthening the clock to five working days for most requesters; the governor vetoed it on April 17, 2025, writing that “all legitimate requests for public transparency under CORA should be treated equally under the law” (Roberts 2025). In March 2026 a third consecutive attempt, SB 26-107, died in the Senate State, Veterans and Military Affairs Committee on a 3-2 vote (Roberts 2026). The three-day clock you will compute below is a political outcome that has to be defended every session, which is one reason a state committee is where Chapter 17 sends you.






TipThe Missing Manual



Most records-request advice assumes your request succeeds the first time. It does not. The first response will be partial, redacted, mis-scoped, extended, or held behind a fee estimate. Warren and colleagues (2025) designed their request tool around exactly this slow, iterative process. Design your tracker the same way. Redactions are metadata: the pattern of what an office blacks out tells you its legal theory before it states one. If three of four releases redact the same paragraph under the same subsection of § 24-72-204, you have a de facto policy you can write about, cite in testimony, or hand to a lawyer.

title: 7  Law
section: 7.3 County practice as the statute at work
text:
7.3 County practice as the statute at work
A statute says what a custodian may do; practice shows what custodians do. Boulder County’s Public Records Archive is a public sample of practice: requests filed by others, their dates, and, for many, the released files. Which subsections of § 24-72-204 does the county actually cite? How often does it take the seven-day extension? Do fee estimates cluster in particular offices? Chapter 4 turns the exemptions cited into a ledger of the remedy pathways each leaves open. MuckRock’s archive of prior releases is a national cousin worth searching before you file (MuckRock Foundation 2024).

title: 7  Law
section: 7.4 The Colorado AI Act as state accountability law
text:
7.4 The Colorado AI Act as state accountability law
Newer state law governs what deployers of algorithms must do. Colorado’s SB 24-205, signed in 2024, was widely described as the first comprehensive state law on “high-risk” AI systems used in consequential decisions such as employment, housing, lending, and insurance. It imposed a duty of reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination, required deployers to run risk-management programs and annual impact assessments, required developers to report discovered discrimination risks to the Attorney General, and gave the Attorney General exclusive enforcement authority (Colorado General Assembly 2024b).
None of that took effect. A special session in August 2025 delayed the Act to June 30, 2026. In May 2026 the General Assembly repealed and reenacted it as SB 26-189, effective January 1, 2027 (Colorado General Assembly 2026). The new law drops the duty of care, the risk-management programs, the impact assessments, and the self-reporting. It keeps developer documentation for deployers, notice to consumers before an automated decision, a plain-language explanation within thirty days of an adverse outcome, rights to correct personal data and to request meaningful human review, three-year record retention, and Attorney General enforcement as a deceptive trade practice, with a cure period until 2030. 
Read the two versions through the installed base (Chapter 2). SB 24-205 bet on oversight through documentation the regulated party writes about itself, the workpapers Chapter 8 examines. SB 26-189 bets on remedy for the individual: an explanation, a correction, a human second look. Neither gives the public the aggregate record that would show a pattern, the gap a records request or a worker observatory (Chapter 10) tries to fill. Chapter 8 compares both with New York City’s Local Law 144 and the federal AI inventories.

title: 7  Law
text:
7.5 Law as constraint
Law also limits what accountability work may try. The federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act was long read broadly enough that violating a website’s terms of service, for example with paired test accounts to audit a housing platform, exposed a researcher to liability. Sandvig v. Barr, brought by the ACLU (American Civil Liberties Union 2019), won a 2020 ruling that a terms-of-service violation alone does not make access unauthorized, and Van Buren v. United States (2021) narrowed the statute further. Litigation can also open what requests cannot: the Dutch SyRI ruling of February 2020 (District Court of The Hague 2020) rested on records a lawsuit forced into view, though discovery material usually stays under a protective order. And records law is neutral on its face. Meeting records that list commenters by name can expose the residents who showed up to object; the infrastructure that enables one use enables every use the statute does not exclude, which is why Chapter 5 treats stewardship as a duty.

title: 7  Law
section: 7.6 Tutorial, part 1: a CORA tracker in SQLite
text:
7.6 Tutorial, part 1: a CORA tracker in SQLite
The schema has four tables. A request can have several responses (partial releases, supplemental productions); a response can include several documents; follow-ups are requester actions (clarifications, fee questions, notices) that shape the record without producing documents.
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

DB_PATH = Path("cora_tracker.sqlite")

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS requests (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    agency TEXT NOT NULL,            -- e.g. 'Boulder County'
    office TEXT NOT NULL,            -- the office that holds the records
    date_submitted TEXT NOT NULL,
    date_closed TEXT,                -- as the archive reports it
    description TEXT NOT NULL,
    regime TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (regime IN ('CORA','CCJRA','FOIA','other')),
    status TEXT NOT NULL
        CHECK (status IN ('open','extended','partial','closed','denied'))
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS responses (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    request_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES requests(id),
    date_received TEXT NOT NULL,
    grounds_cited TEXT,              -- verbatim, e.g. 'C.R.S. 24-72-204(3)(a)(II)'
    fee_estimate REAL,
    documents_count INTEGER
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS followups (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    request_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES requests(id),
    date TEXT NOT NULL,
    type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (type IN
        ('clarification','fee_question','reminder','notice_of_intent','withdrawal')),
    content TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS documents (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    response_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES responses(id),
    filename TEXT NOT NULL,
    sha256 TEXT NOT NULL
);
"""
with sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH) as conn:
    conn.executescript(SCHEMA)
The statutory clock is the column a requester most often forgets to compute. Working days skip weekends and the holidays the custodian observes, so let pandas count them.
import pandas as pd

def cora_clock(date_submitted, holidays=()):
    """Due dates for a CORA request: 3 working days, or 10 if extended."""
    day = pd.offsets.CustomBusinessDay(holidays=list(holidays))
    start = pd.Timestamp(date_submitted)
    return {"due": (start + 3 * day).date().isoformat(),
            "extended_due": (start + 10 * day).date().isoformat()}

print(cora_clock("2027-01-28"))   # a request filed on a Thursday
# => {'due': '2027-02-02', 'extended_due': '2027-02-11'}
print(cora_clock("2027-02-10", holidays=["2027-02-15"]))
# => {'due': '2027-02-16', 'extended_due': '2027-02-25'}
Pass the county’s actual holiday calendar, not the federal one you assume it follows. For an archived request, compare its date_closed with due and extended_due: across many requests, the share closed late measures an office’s practice, not one requester’s luck.

title: 7  Law
text:
7.7 Drafting the letter
Every archived request is someone else’s letter. A CORA letter is four short paragraphs. The tone is formal, specificity is load-bearing, and statutory citations do real work. Bracketed text is yours to fill.

Dear Records Custodian,
Pursuant to the Colorado Open Records Act, C.R.S. § 24-72-201 et seq., I request the following public records maintained by [Boulder County office]:

All contracts, amendments, statements of work, and data-sharing agreements between the County and any vendor of [technology or service], executed between January 1, 2023 and the date of this request;
Policies, procedures, and training materials governing the County’s use of [technology or service] during that period;
Any evaluations, audits, or validation reports concerning [technology or service] delivered to or prepared by the County during that period.

I ask that you waive or reduce any fees because I am a student researcher and will publish my analysis for the public; if estimated fees exceed [amount you choose], please contact me before proceeding. If any portion is withheld, please provide a written statement of the grounds, citing the specific legal authority, and release all reasonably segregable non-exempt portions. Electronic copies are preferred.

The citation shows you know the law. The enumerated categories ask for records, not answers, specific enough to resist dismissal as overbroad. The fee paragraph asks for a discretionary waiver honestly and sets a ceiling so a large estimate pauses the request instead of ending it. The last sentence asks for the written basis of any denial, which you will need if the fourteen-day notice and a court ever come into it.

title: 7  Law
section: 7.8 Tutorial, part 2: from a county PDF to a table
text:
7.8 Tutorial, part 2: from a county PDF to a table
Released records arrive as PDFs. Some are born digital and carry a text layer; others are scans and need optical character recognition (OCR). Try the text layer first. Practice on records the county must produce anyway. State law makes the annual budget one of them: the Local Government Budget Law of Colorado requires a county’s governing body to adopt the budget and make appropriations by ordinance or resolution before the mill levy is certified, and to file a certified copy with the state’s Division of Local Government within thirty days of the start of the fiscal year (C.R.S. §§ 29-1-108, 29-1-113) (Colorado General Assembly 2024a).
Boulder County’s Resolution 2025-058 is that document for 2026: the Board of County Commissioners adopted the budget by summarizing expenditures and revenues for each fund (Board of County Commissioners of Boulder County 2025). It is four pages and born digital.
import re
import pdfplumber   # pip install pdfplumber
import pandas as pd

PDF = "resolution-2025-058.pdf"   # downloaded from bouldercounty.gov
ROW = re.compile(r"^(?P<label>.+?)\s+\$(?P<amount>[\d,]+)$")

rows, section = [], None
with pdfplumber.open(PDF) as pdf:
    for page_no, page in enumerate(pdf.pages, start=1):
        for line in (page.extract_text() or "").splitlines():
            line = line.strip()
            if re.match(r"^Section \d+$", line):
                section = line
            elif (m := ROW.match(line)) and section:
                rows.append({"section": section,
                             "label": m["label"].strip(),
                             "amount": int(m["amount"].replace(",", "")),
                             "page": page_no})

budget = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(budget.shape)
# => (55, 4)
Do not trust those fifty-five rows yet. Budget tables print their own totals, and recomputing them is the cheapest validation in records work.
def check_totals(df):
    out = []
    for sec, g in df.groupby("section"):
        is_total = g["label"].str.startswith("Total")
        out.append({"section": sec,
                    "rows": int((~is_total).sum()),
                    "sum_of_rows": int(g.loc[~is_total, "amount"].sum()),
                    "printed_total": int(g.loc[is_total, "amount"].sum())})
    out = pd.DataFrame(out)
    out["matches"] = out["sum_of_rows"] == out["printed_total"]
    return out

print(check_totals(budget).to_string(index=False))
# =>   section  rows  sum_of_rows  printed_total  matches
# => Section 1    23    745186611      745186611     True
# => Section 2    23    745186611      745186611     True
# => Section 5     6      4181549        4181549     True
The totals match: twenty-three funds summing to $745,186,611 in estimated expenditures. Now compare the fund names across the expenditure and revenue sections of the same document.
s1 = budget.query("section == 'Section 1' and not label.str.startswith('Total')")
s2 = budget.query("section == 'Section 2' and not label.str.startswith('Total')")
print(sorted(set(s1.label) ^ set(s2.label)))
# => ['Health & Human Services', 'Health and Human Services',
# =>  'Qualified Energy Conservation Bond', 'Qualified Energy Conservation Bonds']
The same two funds are spelled differently on different pages of one resolution. That is a linkability failure in miniature, and a join on fund name would silently drop them. For scanned releases, swap the text layer for OCR (pdftoppm, then tesseract) and hash every file you receive into the documents table.






NoteIn the Public Interest



Chapter 2 names remedy as the installed base’s final element, and Chapter 4 builds on it: evidence matters only if it can trigger action. A records response that sits as an unreadable scan on a laptop is not oversight. It is raw material for oversight. The tracker, letter, and extraction notebook are the minimum scaffolding that turns that material into something a reporter can publish, an advocate can cite before a legislative committee, or an attorney can attach to a complaint (Keegan 2026). CORA’s remedies (the notice, the show-cause order, the fee award) make the scaffolding worth building, and they exist because a legislature wrote them and keeps declining to weaken them. The tools advance openness even when no remedy follows: a well-tracked request records what a government said, and when.

title: 7  Law
text:
7.9 Exercises
Exercise 7.1 (Guided, real public data). Choose one or more released requests from Boulder County’s Public Records Archive (https://bouldercountyco.govqa.us/WEBAPP/_rs/supporthome.aspx). Enter each in the tracker with its office, dates requested and closed, outcome, and fees; record any exemptions cited verbatim in grounds_cited, mapped to a subsection of § 24-72-204 where you can; and hash every released file into documents. Add at least five other archived requests to the same office, write a query that flags any closed after extended_due, and note which wording in your chosen request shaped the response.
Exercise 7.2 (Runnable). Download Resolution 2025-058 and reproduce the extraction and total check above. Then point the same notebook at one Board of County Commissioners packet from the county’s meeting portal (https://pub-bouldercounty.escribemeetings.com/) or at the records released for your chosen request. Report which tables extracted cleanly, which failed the total check, and why.
Exercise 7.3 (Statutory reading). Read SB 24-205 and SB 26-189 side by side. In 500 words, list what each requires of a deployer, who can enforce it, and what a member of the public can obtain under it. Name one record that would have existed under the 2024 Act and will not exist under the 2026 one, and say who loses access to it.
Exercise 7.4 (Open-ended; submittable artifact). Identify a public-interest question about a Colorado city, county, or state agency that records could answer but public datasets cannot. In two pages, name the records, the custodian, the subsections of § 24-72-204 you expect to be cited, the fee you expect under the current cap, and what you would do with the records. Draft the letter. File it only if you are prepared to see the request through.

title: 7  Law
text:
7.10 Looking ahead
Records work is slow, and what returns is rarely everything a requester asked for; Chapter 4 takes what was withheld as evidence in its own right. When the problem is the statute itself, the venue is the legislature: Chapter 17 prepares you to testify before a General Assembly committee. The next lineage, accounting (Chapter 8), asks what an independent check on an institution’s own records looks like at national scale.

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
text:
8.1 Audit-washing: exemption in oversight’s clothes
In October 1929, the New York Stock Exchange lost roughly a quarter of its value in a week. Congress spent the next several years arguing about why, and produced two statutes (the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934) that required publicly traded companies to file financial statements examined by an independent auditor. The external audit went from a discretionary service a firm might commission to reassure its banker to a legally mandated act of public verification. The profession that performed it acquired, as part of the bargain, a public interest mandate. A certified public accountant’s client is the company paying the invoice. The duty of care runs to shareholders, lenders, regulators, and everyone downstream of the company’s claims about itself.
That bargain has been renegotiated since. Arthur Andersen signed off on Enron’s financial statements for years before Enron collapsed in 2001; its consulting practice had been earning more from Enron than its audit practice, and its shredded workpapers became the emblem of audit failure. Congress responded with the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, which tightened independence rules and created the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board to audit the auditors. The mandate was recertified under closer supervision.
Keegan (2026) codes accounting as a lineage of oversight: it formalizes “legible records, standardized controls, and independent verification.” Engineering, its partner in this book’s account of assurance, adds testing and incident learning (Chapter 10). The pressure both answer is exemption (Chapter 4) in a particular costume. Lee (1995) describes accountancy’s professional history as “protecting the public interest in a self-interested way,” and Baker (2005) finds the profession’s own pronouncements invoking “the public” as a legitimating abstraction while serving the paying client. Algorithmic auditing is about to repeat that history unless it studies it.
The natural level for this lineage is the nation. Securities law, the Government Accountability Office (GAO), and the inspectors general are federal institutions, and federal agencies now report thousands of uses of AI in their own operations. This chapter’s audit therefore runs on national data, and its frame is the federal government’s own ledger of the algorithms it uses.
Raji and colleagues (2020) propose an internal algorithmic auditing framework borrowed from accounting, aerospace, and medicine. It names five stages (scoping, mapping, artifact collection, testing, reflection) and insists on durable, dated workpapers. A good audit produces documents a reasonable outsider could read a year later and use to reconstruct what was examined, what was found, and what was decided. A bad one produces a one-paragraph attestation.
The federal government has built the first layer of such a record. Executive Order 13960, signed in December 2020, required agencies to inventory their uses of artificial intelligence (Executive Office of the President 2020). OMB Memorandum M-25-21, issued in April 2025, keeps the annual inventory and requires agencies to apply minimum risk-management practices to use cases they judge “high-impact” (Office of Management and Budget 2025). The consolidated 2025 inventory, published on GitHub, lists 3,611 use cases from 41 agencies, 445 of them self-designated high-impact (Office of Management and Budget 2026). The federal auditor has also written the standard such records should meet. GAO’s AI accountability framework organizes its key practices under governance, data, performance, and monitoring, with questions written for auditors and third-party assessors (US Government Accountability Office 2021). When GAO examined the first round of inventories, it found that 15 of the 20 agencies reporting use cases had submitted incomplete or inaccurate information (US Government Accountability Office 2023).
Compare the city and the state. New York City’s Local Law 144, enforced since July 2023, requires employers using automated employment decision tools to commission an independent “bias audit” and publish a summary of selection rates and impact ratios by sex and race/ethnicity (NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection 2023). Goodman and Trehu (2023) use it to illustrate audit-washing: audits whose institutional form looks like oversight but whose content is shallow enough to credential almost any system. Some published LL144 audits are serious. Others are short PDFs that say which tool was audited and little about which data, metric choices, or population. A regime that accepts both as compliant has granted an exemption while appearing to deny one.
Colorado’s AI Act (SB 24-205) went further on paper, placing risk-management and impact-assessment duties on developers and deployers of “high-risk” systems (Colorado General Assembly 2024). It never took effect. A 2025 special session delayed it, and in May 2026 the legislature repealed and reenacted it as SB 26-189, effective January 1, 2027, which drops the impact assessments and risk-management programs and keeps notices, explanations of adverse decisions, rights to correction and human review, and Attorney General enforcement (Colorado General Assembly 2026).  Chapter 7 reads that sequence as state lawmaking. Here it is a lesson in assurance: audit duties are negotiated, delayed, and narrowed long before anyone audits anything.

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
text:
NoteIn the Public Interest



Oversight, as Chapter 4 develops it, needs authority and remedy that an audit cannot supply by itself. Accounting adds what an audit must supply on its own: dated workpapers, separation of audit from consulting, standards fixed before the numbers are seen, and a credential that can be revoked. An algorithmic audit that lacks all four performs oversight rather than providing it, and that performance is how exemption survives inside a regime that looks like regulation. The continuity element of the installed base (Chapter 2) matters for the same reason: an audit that cannot be rerun next quarter because the analyst’s laptop was wiped is, for public purposes, an audit that did not happen. The specific claim of this chapter is that a manifest, a thresholds file, and a changelog are the minimum installed base for independent verification.

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
section: 8.2 Tutorial, part 1: reading the federal ledger
text:
8.2 Tutorial, part 1: reading the federal ledger
Begin where an auditor begins: with the client’s own books. The inventory is a CSV, and its high-impact columns record whether each minimum practice was carried out.
import pandas as pd

INV = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ombegov/"
       "2025-Federal-Agency-AI-Use-Case-Inventory/main/Data/"
       "2025_individually_reported_AI_use_cases.csv")
inv = pd.read_csv(INV, low_memory=False)
print(inv.shape)
# => (3611, 36)   (repository as of May 2026)

hi = inv.query("is_high_impact == 'High-impact' and development_stage == 'Deployed'")
print(len(hi), hi["hi_assessment_completed"].fillna("(blank)").value_counts().to_dict())
# => 227 {'(blank)': 101, 'In-progress': 90, 'Yes': 36}

print(hi.loc[hi["hi_assessment_completed"].isna(), "agency_name"].value_counts().head(2))
# => Department of Veterans Affairs           94
# => National Credit Union Administration     5
Of 227 deployed high-impact uses, 36 report a completed impact assessment. Do not write “101 have no assessment.” A blank is not a “No”; 94 of the blanks come from one agency, which suggests a reporting format rather than 94 separate decisions. An auditor’s next move is a request for the agency’s own inventory and its supporting documents, not a headline.

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
section: 8.3 Tutorial, part 2: a disaggregated audit on national data
text:
8.3 Tutorial, part 2: a disaggregated audit on national data
Gender Shades (Buolamwini and Gebru 2018) showed that a single accuracy number can hide large disparities across intersectional groups. The disaggregated audit is the technique that refuses the single number. You will run one on folktables (Ding et al. 2021), which packages American Community Survey (ACS) microdata into prediction tasks, using fairlearn for disaggregated metrics. The task, ACSIncome, predicts whether a working adult’s income exceeds $50,000. It is deliberately banal. Load it state by state, keeping only the task’s columns, so the national file fits on a laptop.
# pip install folktables fairlearn scikit-learn pandas pyyaml joblib
import pandas as pd
from folktables import ACSDataSource, ACSIncome, state_list

source = ACSDataSource(survey_year="2018", horizon="1-Year", survey="person")
frames = []
for st in state_list:                          # 50 states and Puerto Rico
    raw = source.get_data(states=[st], download=True)
    X, y, _ = ACSIncome.df_to_pandas(raw)
    frames.append(X.assign(label=y.squeeze().to_numpy(), state=st))
acs = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

print(acs.shape, round(acs["label"].mean(), 3))
# => (1664500, 12) 0.369
The first run downloads about 2 GB. state_list has no District of Columbia, so “national” here means fifty states and Puerto Rico. Write that into the manifest. Now recode race from the ACS RAC1P code and sex from SEX:
RAC1P = {1: "White", 2: "Black", 3: "AIAN", 4: "AIAN", 5: "AIAN",
         6: "Asian", 7: "NHPI", 8: "Some other race", 9: "Two or more"}
race = acs["RAC1P"].map(RAC1P).fillna("Unknown")
sex = acs["SEX"].map({1: "Male", 2: "Female"})
features = acs.drop(columns=["label", "state"])
Check every key against the ACS PUMS data dictionary for your vintage. Codes 3 through 5 are three American Indian and Alaska Native categories, which this map collapses. Hispanic origin is a separate variable (HISP) and is not in the task. RAC1P and SEX are also model features in ACSIncome, which is itself a choice an auditor should question. Write all of these down. Then fit the simplest defensible model:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te, r_tr, r_te, s_tr, s_te, st_tr, st_te = train_test_split(
    features, acs["label"], race, sex, acs["state"],
    test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=acs["label"])
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
y_pred = model.predict(X_te)
The model is crude (occupation and birthplace codes are treated as numbers), which is fine: the audit should be method-agnostic.
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
from fairlearn.metrics import (MetricFrame, count, selection_rate,
    false_positive_rate, false_negative_rate,
    demographic_parity_difference, equalized_odds_difference)

sensitive = pd.DataFrame({"race": r_te, "sex": s_te})
mf = MetricFrame(
    metrics={"n": count, "accuracy": accuracy_score,
             "selection_rate": selection_rate,
             "fpr": false_positive_rate, "fnr": false_negative_rate},
    y_true=y_te, y_pred=y_pred, sensitive_features=sensitive)
print(mf.by_group.sort_values("n").round(3))
# =>                            n  accuracy  selection_rate    fpr    fnr
# => NHPI            Female  436.0     0.846           0.128  0.057  0.566
# => NHPI            Male    450.0     0.758           0.282  0.155  0.436
# => ...                                (14 cells in all)
# => White           Male 205533.0     0.754           0.461  0.224  0.271

dpd = demographic_parity_difference(y_te, y_pred, sensitive_features=sensitive)
eod = equalized_odds_difference(y_te, y_pred, sensitive_features=sensitive)
print(f"DPD {dpd:.3f}  EOD {eod:.3f}")
# => DPD 0.481  EOD 0.545
These numbers come from one run with fairlearn 0.14.0, scikit-learn 1.9.1, and pandas 3.0.6. The two summaries are not “the” fairness score. Each is the gap between two cells: Asian men, selected at 0.541, and women of some other race, at 0.061, for parity; the false-negative rates of the same two groups, 0.184 and 0.729, for equalized odds. MetricFrame.by_group is the centerpiece, and its n column tells your reader whether any other number means anything.
A national auditor also asks whether one model serves every state equally. Pass st_te as the sensitive feature and the gap in accuracy between the best and worst state is 0.073 (Utah at 0.809, Wyoming at 0.736).






TipThe Missing Manual



fairlearn will not tell you which parity metric is defensible. Demographic parity asks whether positive predictions are allocated at the same rate across groups; equalized odds asks whether error rates are balanced given the true label. With unequal base rates they cannot both be satisfied, which is a mathematical result, not a political one. Two quieter surprises. First, demographic_parity_difference is the gap between the highest and lowest group, computed over every cell you pass in. Cross state, race, and sex and you get 714 cells, 244 of them with fewer than thirty people, and a parity difference of exactly 1.0: somewhere a tiny cell had everyone selected and another had no one. The headline is set by your smallest group. Second, nothing in the library warns you about small cells. Report n beside every metric, suppress cells below a documented minimum, and say in prose which groups the audit cannot speak to.


Save the evaluation set and the model so the workpaper can verify them:
import joblib
X_te.assign(label=y_te.values, race=r_te.values, sex=s_te.values,
            state=st_te.values).to_csv("data/acs_2018_test.csv", index=False)
joblib.dump(model, "models/logit-v1.joblib")

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
section: 8.4 Tutorial, part 3: from notebook to workpaper
text:
8.4 Tutorial, part 3: from notebook to workpaper
A notebook produced those numbers once. An audit has to produce them on demand, with a record of every decision and a log of what changed between runs. Build this layout:
audit-pipeline/
├── CHANGELOG.md   Makefile   manifest.yaml   thresholds.yaml   audit.py
├── data/      models/      reports/
manifest.yaml is the input contract. A reviewer a year from now should be able to reconstruct the run without guessing.
audit:
  name: "ACSIncome national disaggregated audit"
  run_id: "2027-03-04-001"
  analyst: "your.name@colorado.edu"
dataset:
  source: "ACS PUMS 2018 1-Year, 50 states and Puerto Rico, via folktables ACSIncome"
  local_path: "data/acs_2018_test.csv"
  sha256: "<output of sha256sum>"
  retrieved_on: "2027-03-04"
  recoding: "RAC1P 3-5 collapsed to AIAN; HISP not used; DC not in state_list"
model:
  path: "models/logit-v1.joblib"
  sha256: "<output of sha256sum>"
  description: "StandardScaler + LogisticRegression, random_state=42"
protected_attributes: [race, sex]
strata: [state]           # carried in the file, never passed to the model
min_cell_size: 100
thresholds_file: "thresholds.yaml"
thresholds.yaml carries the decision rules separately, because they change on a different cadence and need their own authority:
demographic_parity_difference: {warn: 0.05, fail: 0.10}
equalized_odds_difference:     {warn: 0.05, fail: 0.10}
adopted: "2027-03-04"
authority: >
  Teaching values. A real audit cites the statute, rule, policy,
  or contract clause that set them, and who may change them.
Most algorithmic audits skip the authority field, which is how thresholds drift without anyone deciding to move them.
audit.py reads the manifest, verifies the hashes, runs the disaggregation, applies the thresholds, and writes a dated report:
import hashlib, json, pathlib, sys
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import joblib, pandas as pd, yaml
from fairlearn.metrics import (MetricFrame, count, selection_rate,
    false_positive_rate, false_negative_rate,
    demographic_parity_difference, equalized_odds_difference)

SUMMARIES = {"demographic_parity_difference": demographic_parity_difference,
             "equalized_odds_difference": equalized_odds_difference}

def sha256_of(path):
    return hashlib.sha256(pathlib.Path(path).read_bytes()).hexdigest()

def verify(m):
    pairs = [("dataset", m["dataset"]["local_path"]), ("model", m["model"]["path"])]
    bad = [k for k, p in pairs if sha256_of(p) != m[k]["sha256"]]
    if bad:
        sys.exit(f"hash mismatch: {bad}")      # no report for unverified inputs

def run_audit(df, model, m):
    attrs = m["protected_attributes"]
    y_true = df["label"]
    X = df.drop(columns=["label"] + attrs + m.get("strata", []))
    y_pred = model.predict(X)
    mf = MetricFrame(metrics={"n": count, "selection_rate": selection_rate,
                              "fpr": false_positive_rate, "fnr": false_negative_rate},
                     y_true=y_true, y_pred=y_pred, sensitive_features=df[attrs])
    by_group = mf.by_group[mf.by_group["n"] >= m["min_cell_size"]]
    summaries = {k: float(f(y_true, y_pred, sensitive_features=df[attrs]))
                 for k, f in SUMMARIES.items()}
    return by_group, summaries

def evaluate(summaries, thresholds):
    out = []
    for name, value in summaries.items():
        rule = thresholds[name]
        level = ("FAIL" if value >= rule["fail"]
                 else "WARN" if value >= rule["warn"] else "PASS")
        out.append({"metric": name, "value": round(value, 4), "level": level})
    return out

def main():
    m = yaml.safe_load(open("manifest.yaml"))
    thresholds = yaml.safe_load(open(m["thresholds_file"]))
    verify(m)
    df = pd.read_csv(m["dataset"]["local_path"])
    by_group, summaries = run_audit(df, joblib.load(m["model"]["path"]), m)
    report = {"run_id": m["audit"]["run_id"],
              "generated_at": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
              "manifest": m, "findings": evaluate(summaries, thresholds),
              "by_group": by_group.reset_index().to_dict(orient="records")}
    pathlib.Path("reports").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    out = pathlib.Path(f"reports/{m['audit']['run_id']}.json")
    out.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2, default=str))
    print(json.dumps(report["findings"], indent=2))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
# => [{"metric": "demographic_parity_difference", "value": 0.4806, "level": "FAIL"},
# =>  {"metric": "equalized_odds_difference", "value": 0.5449, "level": "FAIL"}]
The script refuses to run on inputs whose hashes do not match the manifest, suppresses small cells by a rule written down in advance, and stamps the run in UTC. Each behavior is borrowed from financial audit practice, where a workpaper exists to be legible to someone who was not in the room.
The Makefile is the one-command interface: an audit target that runs python audit.py and a clean target that removes reports/*.json. If a reviewer cannot type make audit and get a report, the pipeline is not reproducible. clean removes generated reports, never inputs. You do not delete workpapers. You archive them. CHANGELOG.md is the narrative companion to the numbers: one dated entry per run_id, recording the input hashes, the threshold adoption date, the fairlearn and scikit-learn versions, and any change in findings with its root cause.
Commit the directory, run make audit, and read the report for what it does not say: which columns were features, whether the model was evaluated on a holdout. A week later, update run_id and run again. Usually nothing moves. Sometimes a library release changes a default and a metric shifts in the third decimal place. The discipline is not preventing drift. It is noticing it, logging it, and deciding whether it changes the conclusion.

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
section: 8.5 Writing the audit for a non-technical reader
text:
8.5 Writing the audit for a non-technical reader
The JSON report is raw material. The audit is what you write around it, and it is the seed of the report genre in Chapter 15. Use four sections.

What the model is, and is not. A logistic regression trained on one year of national ACS data. A teaching artifact, not a procurement recommendation.
Who is in the data. The per-cell counts, with the smallest cells named in prose, including those below min_cell_size that the audit cannot speak to. Audits that silently drop small cells pretend to a completeness they lack.
What the metrics show. The disaggregated table with a plain-language reading of each gap, its threshold level, and its direction, plus the by-state spread.
What the audit rests on. The recoding, the omitted Hispanic-origin variable, the missing District of Columbia, self-reported and sampled survey data, a single vintage and a single holdout. Name each choice and how a second auditor might make it differently.

Section 4 is where audit-washing hides. If the next auditor cannot reproduce your table from your manifest, the audit is not an instrument of oversight. It is a press release.

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
text:
8.6 Exercises
Exercise 8.1 (Guided, laptop, real public data). Run the national ACSIncome audit above end to end, then build the audit-pipeline/ directory, fill manifest.yaml with real hashes from sha256sum, commit it, and run make audit. Submit the repository URL and the generated report. If your numbers differ from the chapter’s, record your library versions and say where the difference enters.
Exercise 8.2 (Guided). One week later, rerun with a new run_id. Write a changelog entry stating the exact fairlearn and scikit-learn versions and what changed, even if nothing did.
Exercise 8.3 (Analytic, real public data). Load the 2025 federal AI use case inventory. For one agency with at least five high-impact use cases, tabulate every hi_ column. In 400 words, assess the agency’s entries against the four principles of GAO’s accountability framework (US Government Accountability Office 2021). Which workpaper is missing? Distinguish blanks from answers, and name the document you would request to resolve each blank.
Exercise 8.4 (Comparative). In 500 words, compare a published LL144 bias audit summary, the Colorado Act as reenacted by SB 26-189, and M-25-21’s high-impact practices on three dimensions: which systems are covered, who performs the assessment, and what is published. Quote each text. Is the LL144 summary audit-washing in Goodman and Trehu’s (2023) sense? Say what evidence would change your verdict.
Exercise 8.5 (Open-ended; submittable artifact). Extend your pipeline with a second folktables task (ACSEmployment or ACSPublicCoverage) or a second sensitive attribute, still national. Rewrite thresholds.yaml so its authority field names a real federal body and the instrument it could use to adopt such thresholds (an OMB memorandum, a NIST standard, a GAO recommendation). Then write the four-section audit memo (about 800 words). It becomes the methods and findings of a report addressed to that body (Chapter 15).

title: 8  Accounting and Auditing
text:
8.7 Looking ahead
A workpaper records what you did. It does not prove that the code does what the workpaper says. Chapter 10 puts this pipeline under test: shape and range checks on a fixture, a regression snapshot, a deliberately introduced bug, a post-incident review, and continuous integration. Engineering also asks who keeps the record when the audited party will not, which is where worker observatories enter.

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.1 A profession that learned from its mistakes
Every data project is a planning document in disguise. It proposes that some slice of the world is worth measuring, some category system worth applying, some decision worth making differently once the analysis is done. Every decision to stop measuring is a planning document too, usually one nobody was invited to read. Planning has spent the last century learning the consequences of both kinds of proposal. Data scientists have not. This chapter borrows from the planners.
The other lineages in this part supply verification (journalism, Chapter 6), record access and remedy (law, Chapter 7), and independent checking and incident review (accounting and engineering, Chapter 8 and Chapter 10). Planning asks different questions: who decided, who was affected, who was in the room, who was not, and whose knowledge of the terrain counts as evidence. Keegan (2026) puts it in infrastructural terms: planning foregrounds how infrastructures allocate benefits and burdens across space and time, and it supplies the participatory repertoires for negotiating who owns, maintains, and can contest durable systems. That makes planning the lineage of ownership, the value Chapter 5 develops.
Planning’s natural level in this book is the county. In Colorado, counties plan under state statute, and in unincorporated areas the county is the land-use authority: it writes the comprehensive plan, administers the land use code, and hears the applications that turn a parcel into a subdivision or a gravel pit. Your running example is Boulder County. Your anchor case is a decision made elsewhere, on a federal spine, through a consolidated city and county: the reconstruction of Interstate 70 through north Denver.
Modern planning is the result of a public fight it mostly lost and then, slowly, learned from. Robert Moses, as Chapter 1 notes, ran New York’s public works for four decades on a specific theory: the public interest could be computed by a qualified expert, expressed as a highway alignment, and imposed on neighborhoods whose residents could not contest it. Jane Jacobs (1961) took the other side, insisting that people who lived on a block knew things no master plan could capture.
Paul Davidoff’s “Advocacy and Pluralism in Planning” (1965) codified the lesson for planning rather than merely against it. There is no single neutral public interest a competent planner discovers through analysis. There are many publics with conflicting interests, and the planner’s job is to make those conflicts legible rather than paper over them with a unitary plan. The profession should supply advocate planners to underserved communities the way the legal profession supplies public defenders.
Advocacy planning did not become the default, but it changed what the default had to argue against. Sherry Arnstein’s “ladder of citizen participation” (1969) gave planners a vocabulary for distinguishing real participation from its counterfeits, from manipulation and therapy at the bottom, through information, consultation, and placation, to partnership, delegated power, and citizen control at the top. Marcus Lane’s intellectual history (2005) traces how participation became a procedural requirement in most Western planning regimes, even when its substance was thin.
You inherit this tradition whenever you work with geographic data. The choropleth expresses a theory about which boundaries matter; the demographic overlay, a theory about which categories count; the stakeholder list, a theory about whose voice will be sought. Planning’s contribution is to name these theories as theories and insist they be defended.

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.2 Boulder County as planner
Colorado law makes it “the duty of a county planning commission to make and adopt a master plan” for unincorporated territory, subject to the county commissioners’ approval, after hearings at which it “shall accept and consider oral and written public comments” (C.R.S. § 30-28-106) (Colorado General Assembly 2024). In Boulder County that document is the Boulder County Comprehensive Plan (BCCP), built on three commitments: channel growth to municipalities, protect agricultural land, and put environmental resources first in land-use decisions (Boulder County, n.d.). The county’s nine-member appointed Planning Commission adopts and amends it. A typical amendment runs as a numbered docket: in December 2022, docket BCCP-22-0002 restored a housing-counseling policy to the plan’s Housing Element after a public hearing, and the Commission’s resolution adopted it under C.R.S. § 30-28-108 and certified it to the Board under § 30-28-109 (Boulder County Planning Commission 2022).
Day to day, the Community Planning & Permitting department turns the plan and the Land Use Code into decisions on applications. Each is a docket with a number (LU-23-0017), a staff recommendation, and, for the larger ones, hearings before the Planning Commission and the Board. Around the City of Boulder, a second plan sits on top: the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, adopted jointly by the city council, the city’s planning board, the county commissioners, and the county’s Planning Commission. Its 2026 major update, docket BVCP-25-0001, shows how many rooms a single decision has. The four bodies held a work session on April 13, 2026 at which “public testimony will not be taken,” a joint public hearing on June 11, and a Board of County Commissioners hearing on June 25 that accepted no further testimony (Boulder County 2026a). 
Which room the public may speak in is itself a planning decision. In spring 2026 county staff limited public comment at two advisory boards, the Parks and Open Space Advisory Committee and the Historic Preservation Advisory Board, to items on the agenda, “bringing it in line with the other boards and commissions,” as a county spokesperson put it (Stephenson 2026). On Arnstein’s ladder, the rule sets which rung residents may reach, and staff set the agenda.

title: 9  Planning
section: 9.3 The Allegheny Family Screening Tool, through a planner’s eyes
text:
9.3 The Allegheny Family Screening Tool, through a planner’s eyes
Chapter 4 takes up the Allegheny Family Screening Tool as a case of exemption: a county risk-scoring system for child-welfare referrals that could not easily be audited from outside. Read the same county case through a planning lens and a different failure surfaces. The tool was designed by social scientists, procured by a county, and deployed on families who were not in the room; neither were the caseworkers whose judgment it was meant to augment. A planner recognizes the lower rungs of Arnstein’s ladder: information transmitted, consultation held, the decision made by the same people who would have made it without consultation. A participation process that does not feed back into who holds authority to change the decision, and that produces no path to remedy (Chapter 2) when it goes wrong, is participation in name only.

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.4 The anchor case: Central 70
Central 70 is the reconstruction and widening of Interstate 70 through the Elyria-Swansea and Globeville neighborhoods of Denver, a consolidated city and county. The Colorado Department of Transportation and the Federal Highway Administration published a final environmental impact statement and a record of decision in 2017 (Colorado Department of Transportation 2017). The project lowered the highway below grade, capped a section with a park, and widened the roadway. It also displaced residents, prompted litigation over its environmental review, and intensified concerns about diesel exposure in neighborhoods already cut in half by the 1960s viaduct. 
Federal money made Central 70 a “major federal action” under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), which required the environmental impact statement, published drafts, comment periods, and written responses to comments. That process is eroding. In 2025 the Council on Environmental Quality withdrew its government-wide NEPA regulations, and the Supreme Court’s decision in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, which began with a Colorado county’s challenge to a Utah rail line, told courts to defer to agencies on how far an environmental review must reach.  The record that let Elyria-Swansea residents contest Central 70 is a record future residents may not get. A Boulder County docket of your choice works for every technique below.

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.5 Stakeholders as a structured document
A stakeholder map lists the parties to a decision and records what each wants, can do, and can see. It reflects the mapper’s theory of whose interests count; writing the theory down makes it contestable. A version-controlled YAML document beats a slide: it reads like prose, diffs in git, and loads into Python.
# stakeholders_i70.yaml
decision:
  name: Central 70 reconstruction and widening
  lead_agencies: [Colorado Department of Transportation, Federal Highway Administration]
  record_of_decision: 2017
  federal_hook: NEPA environmental impact statement
  geography:
    primary_neighborhoods: [Elyria-Swansea, Globeville]
    county: City and County of Denver
    state: CO

stakeholders:
  - id: cdot
    name: Colorado Department of Transportation
    role: lead_agency
    interests:
      - completing federally funded reconstruction on schedule
      - maintaining I-70 freight and commuter capacity
    power: {formal: high, informal: high}   # owns the right of way
    access:
      in_the_room: yes
      documents_produced: [DEIS, FEIS, ROD, mitigation plan]

  - id: elyria_swansea_residents
    name: Elyria-Swansea residents
    role: affected_community
    interests:
      - reducing diesel particulate exposure
      - avoiding displacement
      - retaining neighborhood connectivity
    power: {formal: low, informal: medium}  # organized through associations
    access:
      in_the_room: partially
      documents_produced: [public comments, litigation filings]
A complete map would list twenty to thirty entries, from FHWA and EPA to neighborhood associations, public health researchers, and contractors. Notice what the schema forces. You cannot fill in power.formal without deciding what “formal” means here, or in_the_room without deciding what “the room” is. For Central 70 there were at least five rooms: NEPA scoping meetings, technical advisory committees, city council chambers, federal court, and the offices where alignment decisions were actually made. For a Boulder County docket, list the staff review, the referral agencies, the Planning Commission hearing, and the Board’s hearing, and note which of them take testimony.

title: 9  Planning
section: 9.6 Who was missing from the room
text:
9.6 Who was missing from the room
Once the map exists, write a companion document listing whose perspectives are absent or under-represented, and why. For Central 70, a partial list includes renters whose landlords were compensated but who received nothing; undocumented residents who stayed away from public meetings for reasons unrelated to interest; children whose cumulative diesel exposure was the health outcome at stake but who had no standing in NEPA; and descendants of households displaced by the original viaduct.
A “who was missing” analysis is a design input, not a ritual apology: name whose perspective is missing, then design the analysis to compensate, with data the formal process did not surface or findings published in formats a missing stakeholder could answer. The same method applies to a dataset. When a series is retired, as in the erosion audit of Chapter 5, ask which of its producers, funders, users, and described populations were in the room. Usually the answer is the program office and the budget office.

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.7 The geographic imagination
Planning’s other contribution is the habit of putting decisions on a map. A map is an argument about what counts as “the area,” and every map excludes something its maker thought irrelevant. geopandas extends pandas with a geometry column, with shapely, pyogrio, and pyproj underneath. You will spend more time with pyproj than you expect.
Boulder County publishes its land-use applications as a polygon layer, one shape per parcel per docket, queryable through the county’s ArcGIS REST service (Boulder County 2026b). Pull the larger discretionary applications filed since 2020, and Census county subdivisions from TIGER/Line (U.S. Census Bureau 2024) to place them:
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd
import requests

# Colorado county subdivisions, TIGER/Line 2023; Boulder County is FIPS 013
cousub = gpd.read_file("tl_2023_08_cousub.zip")
boulder = cousub[cousub["COUNTYFP"] == "013"]
# => 5 rows; CRS is EPSG:4269 (NAD83)

LAYER = ("https://maps.bouldercounty.org/arcgis/rest/services/"
         "PLANNING/OP_Accela_Poly/MapServer/0/query")
params = {
    "where": "DocketType IN ('Special Use Review', "
             "'Limited Impact Special Use Review', 'Rezoning') "
             "AND ApplicationDate >= DATE '2020-01-01'",
    "outFields": "CAPID,DocketType,ApplicationDate,ApplicationStatus",
    "outSR": "4326", "f": "geojson",
}
r = requests.get(LAYER, params=params, timeout=60)
r.raise_for_status()
dockets = gpd.read_file(r.text)
dockets["ApplicationDate"] = pd.to_datetime(dockets["ApplicationDate"], unit="ms")
print(dockets.shape, dockets["CAPID"].nunique())
# => (273, 5) 207   (as of October 2026)
Two layers, two coordinate reference systems (CRS). They will plot together without an exception, because matplotlib does not know what a CRS is. Project everything to a common CRS before you join or measure:
crs = "EPSG:26913"            # UTM zone 13N: metres, correct for the Front Range
boulder, dockets = boulder.to_crs(crs), dockets.to_crs(crs)

per_docket = dockets.dissolve(by="CAPID", aggfunc="first").reset_index()
points = per_docket.set_geometry(per_docket.representative_point())
joined = gpd.sjoin(points, boulder[["NAME", "geometry"]], predicate="within")
print(joined.groupby("NAME").size().sort_values(ascending=False))
# => Bald Mountain           61
# => Boulder                 50
# => Longmont                49
# => Upper St. Vrain         37
# => Lafayette-Louisville    10

ax = boulder.plot(color="whitesmoke", edgecolor="gray", figsize=(9, 7))
points.plot(ax=ax, column="DocketType", legend=True, markersize=6)
ax.set_axis_off()
ax.set_title("Boulder County special use and rezoning dockets, 2020-2026\n"
             "County land-use layer; TIGER/Line 2023 county subdivisions")
The mountain subdivisions carry more discretionary dockets than the plains. That is a descriptive statement about where the county’s planning decisions happen, not a causal claim, and it says nothing yet about who lives there. Adding an ACS 5-year block-group table for Boulder County (Exercise 9.3) puts people on the map; the map’s job is to make the spatial question visible, not to close it.






TipThe Missing Manual



When geopandas breaks, the traceback can come from any of several libraries you did not import, and the most common failure, a CRS mismatch, produces no traceback at all. Always call .to_crs() before you join, buffer, measure, or plot. Three surprises are specific to county planning data. First, one docket can span several parcels, so the layer has 273 shapes for 207 dockets; count CAPID, not rows, or dissolve first. Second, ArcGIS REST returns dates as milliseconds since 1970, which is why the code converts them. Third, check the newest date before you treat a layer as current. In October 2026 the most recent application in this layer was dated May 4, 2026, although records were still being edited. A quiet layer may mean a quiet docket, a migration to a new permitting system, or a stalled sync; only the county can say which.  The layer also carries owner names. Do not request fields you do not need.

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.8 Community-informed categorization
The demographic columns you add to the map are themselves planning artifacts. “Percent below poverty line” is a federal category with a specific history. “Two or more races” did not exist as a Census response option before 2000. Bowker and Star (2000), whose work returns in Chapter 13, show that category systems that once fit the world come to shape what the world is allowed to look like. Planning categories do too: “Limited Impact Special Use Review” decides how much public process an application gets.
Community-informed categorization treats category choice as participatory. If the community you are mapping has its own neighborhood or mountain-town boundaries that do not match Census geography, include both, labeled. If a dimension residents care about (length of residence, wildfire rebuild status, primary language at home) is not in the standard tables, say so in the caption rather than pretending it does not exist. Treating the power to categorize as something held in trust, rather than exercised unilaterally, is the bridge from planning to ownership.






NoteIn the Public Interest



Keegan (2026) defines ownership as collective, accountable governance over how public-relevant data is preserved, accessed, and used, and Chapter 5 builds it out. Planning is where that value gets procedural teeth. The specific claim: a community that cannot contest the map on which its land use was planned, or find the docket that changed it, has no ownership of its own record in any meaningful sense, whatever the license says. A county that publishes its dockets as a queryable layer, with numbers that link to staff reports and resolutions, has built part of that installed base; a county that limits where residents may speak has narrowed it. Audit-washing (Chapter 8) has a planning cousin, participation-washing: the map is drawn, the meeting is held, comments are noted, and the decision proceeds as if none of it occurred. Ask whether any document you produce could change the decision, or whether it was always going to be filed.

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.9 Exercises
Exercise 9.1 (Guided). Build a stakeholder map in YAML for a Boulder County decision (a docket from the land-use layer, a BCCP amendment, or the BVCP update) or for Central 70. Include at least ten entries and list every room in which the decision was discussed, noting which took testimony. Commit it as exercises/ch09_stakeholders_<slug>.yaml with a two-paragraph README.md stating the decision, the records you used, and what you could not find.
Exercise 9.2 (Analytic). Write a 400-word “who was missing from the room” analysis of the decision in Exercise 9.1. Name at least four groups and, for each, the document or outreach method that would have surfaced them. If you instead studied a dataset’s retirement in Chapter 5, apply the same method to it, with roles for producer, funder, mandate, downstream user, described population, and mirror.
Exercise 9.3 (Technical, laptop, real public data). Reproduce the docket map above. Then add a third layer: an ACS 5-year block-group variable for Boulder County, joined to TIGER/Line block-group geometry. Project to a common CRS, document the choice in the caption, and write two sentences on what the overlay shows and what it cannot.
Exercise 9.4 (Reflective). Reread Eubanks’s (2018) Allegheny chapter, which Chapter 4 discusses, or read her Indiana eligibility chapter. Apply her framework to your Exercise 9.1 case. Where does the decision’s theory of the problem locate the cause of harm? Where would Eubanks locate it? What would change in your stakeholder map if you adopted her framing? 500 words.
Exercise 9.5 (Open-ended; submittable artifact). Design a participatory process that could have produced a materially different outcome for your Exercise 9.1 decision. Name the rung of Arnstein’s ladder it would occupy, who would hold what authority, and the minimum infrastructure (time, money, translation, childcare, data access, legal support) it would require. Then answer the harder question: what would have had to be true about the county, the applicant, or the political moment for it to happen? 750 words. The analysis is the evidence base for a public comment to the Planning Commission or Board (Chapter 18).

title: 9  Planning
text:
9.10 Looking ahead
Planning gave you the habit of asking who was in the room and whose knowledge of the terrain counts. Chapter 5 turns that habit into an obligation to steward the record, and Chapter 18 turns it into a genre addressed to a county board. The next lineage, engineering (Chapter 10), returns to the national audit and asks a narrower question with the same spirit: when something fails, who keeps the record of how?
