title: 16  Research Proposals
text:
16.1 The grant-proposal genre landscape
The op-ed in Chapter 14 argued for a thing that already exists; the report in Chapter 15 documented a thing that had already happened. The research proposal is stranger than either. It argues, in the present tense, for the significance of work that does not yet exist, using evidence you cannot yet produce, on behalf of findings you cannot yet guarantee, to readers who will decide whether the work should exist at all. You are asking a funder to believe in a future that is currently a document.
The proposal is also the genre that most often grows out of the others. A report whose methods section listed what the audit could not support (Chapter 15), or a public comment a planner answered with “we don’t have that data” (Chapter 18), points toward a larger study someone would have to pay for. Unlike the other genres in Part IV, the proposal has no natural level of government: its reader is a funder, and the level comes from the body your impact paragraph names. Its “gap” and “approach” moves, situating work in a literature and defending a method against it, are also what a skeptical reader of any artifact will ask of you.
The hard part is translating a public-interest data question into a shape a funder can recognize, and translating your own working life into a budget a program officer can defend to a board. By the end of the chapter you will have the documents a proposal package is made of: a one-page specific-aims document, an approach section grounded in a literature matrix, a budget with a narrative justification, a data management plan (DMP), and a draft Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocol, assembled for a named funder’s open call.
The funders you might realistically approach divide into four ecologies, each with its own vocabulary and its own review cycle.
Federal science and humanities agencies include NSF, NIH, IMLS, and NEH. They publish detailed proposal guides (National Science Foundation 2024), use peer-review panels, require formal budgets with indirect-cost recovery, and expect data management plans and broader-impacts sections. As of 2025 they are volatile ground: appropriations uncertainty and agency restructuring mean a proposal submitted under one quarter’s rules may be reviewed under the next’s (Institute of Museum and Library Services 2024; National Endowment for the Humanities 2024; National Institutes of Health 2024).
National private foundations include Knight, MacArthur, Ford, and Robert Wood Johnson. They run on program cycles, usually expect a letter of inquiry first, and keep review standards less public than NSF’s; you are writing for a program officer who is writing for a board (John S. and James L. Knight Foundation 2024).
Regional and community foundations include the Gates Family Foundation in Colorado, the Boettcher Foundation, the Denver Foundation, and analogues in every state (Gates Family Foundation 2024; Boettcher Foundation 2024). Grants run smaller (often $10,000 to $75,000), cycles are shorter, and priorities are locally specific. For a first public-interest research proposal, they are often the right target.
University seed grants are the quietest and often the most accessible category: a $5,000 to $25,000 pilot on a two-page application, and a pilot result is the strongest leverage for the next proposal.

title: 16  Research Proposals
section: 16.2 The political economy of what gets funded
text:
16.2 The political economy of what gets funded
The gap between the money available for public-interest research and the projects that could usefully spend it is large, and a typical program officer declines most of the projects they would like to fund. Two implications follow. Specificity beats scope: a proposal promising to solve algorithmic discrimination in public-benefits systems will lose to one promising to audit the adverse-action notices issued by one county’s SNAP system over eighteen months. Work already pinned to a named body (a city council, a county planning commission, a state legislative committee, a federal agency) arrives at the proposal with its scope half-written. And if your specific aims are not legible in ninety seconds, your proposal will not get the second read.
Political economy also shapes what counts as “research.” A community-engaged audit whose primary output is a community report is harder to fund through NSF than through a regional foundation. A refusal specification whose output is a decision not to build a dataset is harder to fund than either. Part of the proposal-writing work is finding the funder for whom your project is recognizable.

title: 16  Research Proposals
section: 16.3 The specific-aims page as sales pitch
text:
16.3 The specific-aims page as sales pitch
The specific-aims page is the most important page of any research proposal: the first thing a reviewer reads, often the last, and the basis of an opinion that is then difficult to move. The report’s executive summary from Chapter 15 is its closest sibling, but runs the opposite direction: the executive summary distills work already done; the specific-aims page promises work not yet done and argues that it is worth paying for.
A conventional specific-aims page has four moves. First, a significance paragraph naming the public-interest problem in the vocabulary the funder uses. Second, a gap paragraph naming what is not yet known, or audited, or refused. Third, two or three numbered aims, each with a one-sentence hypothesis or deliverable. Fourth, an impact paragraph naming the actors who will act on the results. If the proposal grows out of an earlier artifact, those actors are usually the body that artifact addressed: the city council, the federal agency, the state legislative committee, the county planning commission.
First-time authors miss the first move most often. The significance paragraph is not a general statement about why data matters; it is a claim written in the exact vocabulary of the funder’s open call. If the NSF program says “trustworthy AI,” your first paragraph says “trustworthy AI.” If the Knight Foundation call says “local news ecosystems,” your first paragraph says “local news ecosystems.” This is translation, not cynicism.






TipThe Missing Manual



The specific-aims page is not a summary. It is a sales pitch, written in the vocabulary of the field you are selling to, by a person who has read the funder’s last three years of awards and knows what rhymes with them. Rewrite it five times, once as if you were the skeptic on the review panel. Show each draft to a colleague outside your topic and ask what you are proposing and why a funder should care. If they cannot tell you, the page is not done. And: the budget narrative matters more than the budget numbers. A plausible story about personnel time beats a precise calculation that assumes the work will take half as long as it will. Reviewers have seen the half-time calculation. They are not impressed by it.

title: 16  Research Proposals
text:
16.4 Budgets and justifications
A proposal budget has three components. Personnel covers salary and fringe for the people doing the work (PI, co-investigators, graduate students, hourly undergraduates, a contracted community liaison). Direct costs cover everything else accounted for line by line (software licenses, compute credits, travel, honoraria, transcription, modest equipment). Indirect costs, or facilities and administration (F&A), are overhead the institution charges to keep the lights on. Federal indirect rates at research universities run from roughly 25 to 65 percent of modified total direct costs; foundations often cap indirects at 10 to 15 percent, and some refuse them entirely.
A simple one-year, $50,000 project budget, at a regional foundation that caps indirects at 15 percent, might look like this:
import pandas as pd

budget = pd.DataFrame([
    {"category": "Personnel", "item": "PI (0.10 FTE, summer)", "amount": 14000},
    {"category": "Personnel", "item": "Graduate RA (0.25 FTE, 9 mo)", "amount": 15000},
    {"category": "Personnel", "item": "Fringe benefits (22%)", "amount": 6380},
    {"category": "Direct", "item": "Community-liaison honorarium", "amount": 3000},
    {"category": "Direct", "item": "Participant honoraria (10 x $75)", "amount": 750},
    {"category": "Direct", "item": "Compute and storage (AWS / Zenodo)", "amount": 1200},
    {"category": "Direct", "item": "Travel (2 site visits)", "amount": 1500},
    {"category": "Direct", "item": "Publication and open-access fees", "amount": 1650},
    {"category": "Indirect", "item": "F&A at 15% of MTDC", "amount": 6520},
])

totals = budget.groupby("category")["amount"].sum()
print(totals)
# => Direct        8100
#    Indirect      6520
#    Personnel    35380
#    Name: amount, dtype: int64
print("Total:", budget["amount"].sum())
# => Total: 50000
The numbers are not the hard part; the narrative justification is. Every line needs a sentence or two in a companion document saying what the money pays for and why that level of effort is necessary. The graduate RA line is not “0.25 FTE for nine months at the university rate.” It is “25 percent effort over nine academic months to conduct the FOIA log coding, build the reproducible pipeline described in Aim 2, and co-author the final community report.” A reviewer should come away knowing what each person will do on a Tuesday afternoon. Write the narrative first and fit the numbers to it.

title: 16  Research Proposals
text:
16.5 The data management plan
Federal funders require a data management plan (DMP) in every proposal, and foundations increasingly ask for one (California Digital Library 2024). The DMP is not a formality: it tells the funder, in two pages, what data your project will produce, where it will live, who can access it, for how long, and under what conditions. The DMPTool, operated by the California Digital Library, provides templates for most major funders (California Digital Library 2024).
A serviceable DMP covers six sections.
Types of data. What you will collect or generate. Be specific. “Administrative data from the Colorado Department of Human Services under a data use agreement” is specific. “Public records” is not.
Formats and standards. CSV, Parquet, GeoJSON, JSON-LD, whatever applies. If you follow a community standard (HUD’s HMIS data dictionary, or the FAIR Guiding Principles (Wilkinson et al. 2016)), name it.
Storage during the project. University-managed storage under a DUA, encrypted at rest, with access restricted to named project personnel.
Retention and destruction. How long you keep the data, and what you do with it at the end. A state-agency DUA typically requires destruction of identifiable data within ninety days of project close.
Sharing. What you will make public, and where. A de-identified derived dataset on Zenodo (CERN 2024) with a CC-BY license and a DOI; a code repository on GitHub linked from the dataset record; a datasheet following Gebru and colleagues (Gebru et al. 2021). If something will not be shared, say why.
Preservation. Where the shared outputs live after you stop paying attention. Name a repository that mints a DOI, such as Zenodo, as the deposit of record (Chapter 19); an Internet Archive mirror is a useful second copy. A GitHub repo you maintain is not a preservation plan.
The DMP is where you operationalize the installed base for your own project: linkability in formats and standards, interpretability in the datasheet, continuity in preservation, safe scrutiny in sharing.

title: 16  Research Proposals
section: 16.6 The IRB protocol as a sibling genre
text:
16.6 The IRB protocol as a sibling genre
The IRB protocol sits beside the proposal but is not part of it: a risk document, read by a different office, arguing that the work will not harm the humans it touches.
The framing texts are the Belmont Report (National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research 1978) and the revised Common Rule (US Department of Health and Human Services 2018). Belmont’s three principles (respect for persons, beneficence, justice) structure every IRB form. Your local IRB (at CU Boulder, the Office of Research Integrity (University of Colorado Boulder Office of Research Integrity 2024)) operationalizes them through a protocol template covering population, recruitment, consent, data handling, risks, benefits, and conflicts of interest.
Public-interest data science often works at the edge of IRB jurisdiction. An audit of administrative data under a DUA may be “not human subjects research.” A community survey unambiguously requires full review. A scrape of public social-media posts lands in a contested middle ground whose answer depends on your institution, your IRB chair, and the year. When in doubt, ask: an IRB that tells you a project is exempt is a better friend than one that reads about it in the press.

title: 16  Research Proposals
section: 16.7 Community-engaged research as a proposal-design problem
text:
16.7 Community-engaged research as a proposal-design problem
If the work involves a community partner (a neighborhood association, a legal-aid clinic, a union local, a tribal nation’s data office), the proposal has a different shape. The partner is a collaborator, not a subject; their time is an in-kind contribution or a subcontracted line item; their name belongs on the proposal; their data governance sets the terms.
Costanza-Chock’s design-justice framing (Costanza-Chock 2020) and the CARE Principles for Indigenous data governance (Carroll et al. 2020) are the two sources most worth reading before you draft a community-engaged proposal. They change the budget (honoraria become line items), the DMP (data-sovereignty provisions become load-bearing), and the aims (the community’s question is Aim 1).

title: 16  Research Proposals
section: 16.8 The approach section and the literature matrix
text:
16.8 The approach section and the literature matrix
A review panel asks one question of every approach section: why this method, given what the field already knows? A strong answer has three parts. Situate the work in at least five scholarly sources, saying what each claims and where your project agrees or departs. Name one methodological choice (a metric, a sampling frame, a unit of analysis, a decision not to collect) and the alternative the literature would favor. Defend your choice, or concede it, in light of that literature.
A literature matrix keeps the section honest. Here is one for a proposal that grows out of a disaggregated audit (Chapter 8) whose key choice was to report false positive rate gaps rather than calibration:
import pandas as pd

matrix = pd.DataFrame([
    {"key": "buolamwini2018", "claim": "Disaggregation exposes intersectional error gaps",
     "stance": "supports"},
    {"key": "chouldechova2018", "claim": "A deployed county tool shows metric choices in practice",
     "stance": "complicates"},
    {"key": "raji2020", "claim": "Audits need an end-to-end accountability frame",
     "stance": "supports"},
    {"key": "goodman2023", "claim": "Audits can launder systems they claim to check",
     "stance": "challenges"},
    {"key": "selbst2019fairness", "claim": "Metric choice abstracts away social context",
     "stance": "challenges"},
])

print(len(matrix), "sources")
# => 5 sources
print(matrix["stance"].value_counts())
# => stance
#    supports       2
#    challenges     2
#    complicates    1
#    Name: count, dtype: int64
The check that matters is the last one. A matrix in which every source “supports” your choice is a reading list, not a literature review. If nothing challenges you, you have not read far enough. The matrix is also the seed of the specific-aims page’s gap paragraph: the place where the challenging sources leave a question open is the place your next study lives.

title: 16  Research Proposals
text:
16.9 Broader impacts, taken seriously
NSF requires a broader-impacts section; most private foundations require something analogous. First-time authors treat these as boilerplate, and reviewers read past it.
The strong version asks who will be better off if the project succeeds, in a way that would not have happened otherwise, and names the partners, open datasets, reproducible code, and training opportunities that make it so. It ties to the ownership question from Chapter 5: whose problem is this, and who gets to act on the answer? And it anticipates the sustainability question from Chapter 11: when the grant money is gone, does the infrastructure continue, or evaporate with your last invoice?






NoteIn the Public Interest



The broader-impacts section is where “public interest” becomes concrete and accountable. Tie it explicitly to ownership as you built it in Chapter 5: the community whose data you are using is a partner with a stake in the outcomes, not a population to be studied. And tie it to sustainability as you interrogated it in Chapter 11: a funded pilot that dies when the grant ends has not advanced the installed base; it has spent the trust of staff and community members who will be asked to engage the next pilot with less of it. A section that names the partners, the deliverables they will own at the end, and the maintenance plan that survives the grant is one a reviewer will remember. A section that promises mentorship and open access without naming who, by whom, or where reads as filler.

title: 16  Research Proposals
text:
16.10 Exercises
Exercise 16.1 (Structural reading, real public data). Query the NSF Awards API (https://api.nsf.gov/services/v1/awards.json) with requests for a keyword close to your project (for example "public interest technology", "open government data", or "algorithmic accountability"), load the award list into a pandas DataFrame, and keep id, title, awardeeName, fundsObligatedAmt, startDate, and abstractText. Pick three abstracts and mark where significance, gap, aims, and impact appear. In 400 words, describe how the aims echo the program’s vocabulary. Save the notebook and exercises/ch16_nsf_aims_diagram.md.
Exercise 16.2 (Literature matrix and approach section). For a project that grows out of an artifact you have already produced (or a question from any chapter of this book), build the literature matrix from this chapter with at least five sources, at least one of which challenges your key methodological choice. Write a 750-to-1,000-word approach section from it. Save as proposal/approach.md.
Exercise 16.3 (Specific-aims page). Draft a one-page specific-aims document for a one-year, $50,000 study. Target a plausible funder at the right scale: the Gates Family Foundation, the Boettcher Foundation, a university seed-grant program, or another funder with an open call. Read three of its recent awards first. Use the four-move structure and name, in the impact paragraph, the government body that will act on the results. Rewrite five times. Save the fifth draft as proposal/specific_aims.md.
Exercise 16.4 (Budget and DMP). Produce a budget (adapt the pandas example or write proposal/budget.csv) with personnel, direct costs, and indirects at the funder’s actual cap, and a one-page narrative justification. Then draft a two-page DMP with the DMPTool template (California Digital Library 2024), covering all six sections, naming the datasheet standard (Gebru et al. 2021), and naming as the preservation host a Zenodo record and DOI of the kind Chapter 19 shows you how to create. Save as proposal/budget_justification.md and proposal/dmp.md.
Exercise 16.5 (Submittable artifact: a proposal package for a named funder). Draft an IRB protocol covering consent, risk, data handling, benefits, and conflicts of interest, grounded in the Belmont Report (National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research 1978) and the revised Common Rule (US Department of Health and Human Services 2018); if the project is probably exempt, say so and explain why. Then assemble a package with three parts:

Technical artifact. A runnable repository containing the NSF Awards notebook from 16.1 (or an equivalent query of your target funder’s public award data), the budget script and CSV, and any pilot analysis the aims page cites, so a reviewer can reproduce every number in the package.
Public text. The specific-aims page, approach section, budget justification, DMP, and IRB protocol, formatted to the target funder’s current guidelines and ready to upload to its portal or attach to a letter of inquiry.
Provenance, gaps, and AI-use note (about 300 words). Which pressure does the proposed study answer? Which installed-base elements (Chapter 2) would it build, and which would remain missing when the grant ends? Disclose how you used AI tools in drafting.

Submit it in the funder’s next cycle, after your sponsored-research office reviews the budget.

title: 16  Research Proposals
text:
16.11 Closing
A proposal is a promise about future work, and a promise is only as good as the record it leaves. The genres on either side of this chapter put evidence into public records now: testimony to a state committee (Chapter 17) and a comment on a county docket (Chapter 18). Chapter 19 turns any of that work into a deposit with a DOI. Chapter 20 asks what the whole framework, including the proposal genre’s habit of translating every problem into fundable aims, cannot see.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
17.1 What testimony is and is not
A legislative committee room is an unusual venue for data science. At the Colorado State Capitol, the General Assembly’s guide to public hearings asks that you not cheer, boo, or applaud, that you leave signs and placards outside, and that you not wear clothing that announces a position on a bill before the committee (Colorado General Assembly, n.d.). You sign up to testify through the legislature’s website, in person or remotely. Your laptop is closed. The committee sits at the front, the bill’s sponsor has presented it, and the chair calls witnesses. When the chair calls your name, a clock starts, and when it runs out you will not get the extra thirty seconds you wish for.
Testimony is a genre. Like the op-ed in Chapter 14 and the report in Chapter 15, it has conventions you can learn and a specific theory of what counts as contribution. Unlike those genres, it is also a performance, delivered in public and preserved in the record of a governing body. A well-argued op-ed persuades at scale. A well-argued report becomes institutional evidence. Testimony becomes voice in the record: a durable, citable mark that a particular person said a particular thing to a particular body on a particular day. The genre’s rules follow from that.
This chapter sets testimony at the state level, where law is made. The legal lineage (Chapter 7) treats statutes such as the Colorado Open Records Act (CORA) as the rules that decide what the public can see and what remedies it has when a custodian says no. Those rules are changed in the General Assembly, and committee hearings are where the public speaks to the people changing them. You will need evidence: a tracker of released records requests and an extraction notebook (Chapter 7), and a ledger of the exemptions custodians cited and the remedies each leaves open (Chapter 4). From that evidence you will write a timed oral statement of about three minutes, a written statement of about 1,000 words for the record, and prepared answers to the questions you can anticipate. The mechanics transfer: congressional hearings, county boards, and European parliamentary consultations share a common structure even when the clocks differ.
An op-ed is persuasion at scale; you do not know your reader, and the outlet is the introduction. A report is institutional evidence; the sponsor’s imprint carries you. Testimony is neither. It is voice. At a congressional hearing, a committee invites you because of who you are, and witness selection signals which perspectives it wants on the record. At a Colorado General Assembly committee hearing on a bill, nobody has to invite you. You are a resident, a student, or a researcher who signed up. That is a strength as well as a limit: the committee hears from you because the process is open to the public, not because a staffer chose you.
Four features distinguish testimony from the book’s other genres:
Frances Haugen’s October 2021 appearance before a Senate Commerce subcommittee is a useful genre case at the federal level (Haugen 2021). Read the transcript twice. The first time, notice how much of it is about Haugen: her training, the team she worked on, the internal research she saw. The personal voice is load-bearing; without it, the claim that the company knew about its products’ harms is an assertion, and with it the claim is a witness account. The second time, mark every specific ask. There are fewer than you expect, and they are not buried. Compare her with the civil-society organizations that submitted evidence during the negotiation of the EU AI Act. Their voice was institutional rather than personal, their texts were longer, and their asks were often line edits to draft articles. Both are testimony. The difference lies in who is speaking and what the body can change.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
Voice. You speak in the first person, name your affiliation and your relationship to the issue, and state the claim you came to make. An op-ed can be abstracted from its author; testimony cannot.
Brevity. Five minutes is a congressional convention. State committees are often shorter, and the chair may limit each witness’s time to fit the hearing. Whatever the clock, it is shorter than you want.
A specific ask. Testimony that does not end in a request the committee can act on is a lecture. A committee of reference can vote a bill up or down, adopt an amendment, or send it on to another committee. Ask for one of those things, and when you sign up, say whether you are for, against, or seeking an amendment.
Questions. Committee members may question witnesses after they speak. The exchange also continues afterward, with staff, the sponsor, lobbyists, and reporters, and you need answers ready.








NoteIn the Public Interest



Oversight, as Chapter 4 defines it, needs authority and remedy, and a legislature is where both are written. CORA’s exemptions and its remedies (a written denial, a notice of intent, a district court action) exist because a General Assembly enacted them, and a later General Assembly can widen or narrow them. Testimony is how evidence about how those rules work in practice reaches the people who can change them, in public. Written testimony submitted through the legislature’s website becomes part of the public record (Executive Committee of the Legislative Council, Colorado General Assembly 2025), a public document (Chapter 7) that a reporter, a future requester, or a litigant can cite years from now. The specific claim of this chapter is that testimony advances oversight only when it pairs a verifiable finding with an ask the committee in the room has the authority to grant; testimony addressed to the wrong level of government is a complaint with good production values. Chapter 19 takes up the deposit that keeps your version available even if the legislature’s website changes.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
17.2 The scenario
For the rest of the chapter, imagine that a bill before a committee of the Colorado General Assembly would amend CORA in two ways: it would require every records custodian to publish a log of request outcomes, including the statutory grounds for any denial, and it would require state agencies to publish a register of the automated decision tools they use. This bill and its hearing are hypothetical. For your own testimony, you will target a real bill during the legislative session, or a topic before an interim committee, and your ask will follow from your own evidence.
Know the calendar before you write a word. The General Assembly must convene its regular session no later than the second Wednesday in January and must adjourn within 120 calendar days (Office of Legislative Legal Services, Colorado General Assembly, n.d.). Under Article V, Section 20 of the Colorado Constitution (the GAVEL amendment), every bill referred to a committee of reference must be considered on its merits and voted on, so a bill you care about will get a hearing; the question is when. Hearing notices appear in the daily House and Senate calendars, and the legislature warns that hearings are often delayed or rescheduled (Executive Committee of the Legislative Council, Colorado General Assembly 2025). Look up the current rules for your hearing, and write a three-minute statement that can grow if the chair allows, not a five-minute statement that has to be amputated at the table.
Remember, too, who usually speaks. Einstein, Palmer, and Glick (2019), coding minutes from local planning and zoning meetings, found that commenters were disproportionately older, male, and homeowners compared with the communities they lived in. A weekday hearing in Denver during the session has its own filters: time off work, travel, and familiarity with the process. If your testimony concerns people who rarely come to these rooms (families screened by a human-services tool, people held in county jails), say so, and do not claim to speak for them.

title: 17  Testimony
section: 17.3 A pandas detour that earns one sentence
text:
17.3 A pandas detour that earns one sentence
Testimony that rests on impressions does not survive questioning. You need one or two facts that are yours, defensible, and citable. The hypothetical bill would require every custodian to publish what some already do: Boulder County posts requests it has answered, with the released records, in the Public Records Archive of its Open Records Center (Chapter 7). That is both evidence of feasibility and a dataset. The remedy ledger you build in Chapter 4 codes each archived request’s outcome, the grounds cited, and whether the response came after the statutory clock.
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

with sqlite3.connect("remedy_ledger.sqlite") as conn:
    req = pd.read_sql("SELECT request_id, office, outcome, past_clock "
                      "FROM requests", conn)

summary = (req.groupby("outcome")
              .size()
              .reindex(["full", "partial", "denied", "none", "fee_hold"],
                       fill_value=0))
print(summary.to_dict(), "of", len(req))
print(f"past the statutory clock: {req['past_clock'].mean():.0%}")
# => {'full': ..., 'partial': ..., 'denied': ..., 'none': ..., 'fee_hold': ...} of n
# => past the statutory clock: ...%
That gives you a sentence you can say aloud, and it should claim exactly what the ledger supports: “Of the [n] requests to [office] posted in Boulder County’s own Public Records Archive that I coded, [k] came back in full, [k] were partly withheld, and [k] cited trade-secret protection for vendor contracts.” The second fact is legal, not numerical, and comes from Chapter 7: CORA gives a requester who is denied no administrative appeal; the path runs from a written denial through a notice of intent to district court. Pair them and you have the spine of an argument: one county already publishes outcomes, the outcomes show a pattern worth seeing statewide, and without a published log a requester elsewhere cannot tell whether a denial is routine or unusual before deciding whether to go to court.
A hostile listener can ask you to show your work, and you can: the written statement’s footnotes link to the repository and the commit. This is the clearest answer to “why learn pandas if my goal is policy work.” One well-sourced sentence in the record is worth more than a page of assertion, and code is how you produce the sentence and prove it.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
17.4 The timed oral statement
Here is a structure for three minutes. Deviate from it deliberately, not by accident.
[0:00-0:20]  Your name, where you live or study, the bill number,
             and your position, in two sentences.
[0:20-0:50]  One concrete finding. A number, a custodian, a date.
[0:50-2:00]  The argument: why current law fails the public.
             Two beats, not more.
[2:00-2:40]  The ask, in one sentence. Then say it again.
[2:40-3:00]  Thank the committee. Stop talking.
If the chair allows more time, expand the middle, not the ends: add a second finding, one sentence on what the bill does well, and the specific amendment language you want. Do not add to the introduction. Your credentials are the least interesting thing about your statement.
Your first sentence should fit in one breath. “Thank you, Chair and members of the committee. My name is [name]; I am a student at the University of Colorado Boulder and a Boulder County resident, and I am here in support of [bill number] with one amendment” is fine, but only if the next sentence is specific.






TipThe Missing Manual



Four things guides to testifying rarely say. First, remote registration closes when the hearing on the bill begins, and only registered witnesses are admitted to the Zoom meeting; a link forwarded by a friend will not get you in (Executive Committee of the Legislative Council, Colorado General Assembly 2025). Second, registering does not guarantee you will be heard: the chair may limit total testimony, limit each witness’s time, and call witnesses in any order, and remote witnesses with technical problems may be skipped. If that happens, the legislature lets you submit written testimony on its website until the hearing closes. Third, the record is narrower than you might assume. The legislature archives live and archived audio of committee hearings, but video of remote testimony is not broadcast or recorded, so your words survive and your slides do not. Fourth, hearings slip. A bill scheduled for 1:30 may be heard at 6:00, or laid over. Bring your printed statement, a charger, and patience, and send the written version whether or not you get to speak.

title: 17  Testimony
section: 17.5 The written statement for the record
text:
17.5 The written statement for the record
The written statement is what a reporter will quote, what a future requester will find, and what a lawyer might attach to a filing. It runs about 1,000 words, with footnotes. The oral statement says the thing. The written statement shows the work.

Identification. Name, affiliation, relationship to the issue, the bill number, and your position (support, oppose, or amend).
The problem. Two short paragraphs. What residents cannot currently learn, and why it matters.
The finding. The facts you are there to put on the record, with a table from your ledger and links to the data and code.
Analysis of the bill. Where it is sound, where it is too narrow or too vague, and proposed amendment language where you have it, keyed to the bill’s section numbers.
Response to the likely objection. Usually cost to custodians or the burden on small local governments. Answer it in a paragraph, citing a comparable practice if you can; the county archive is one.
The ask. Explicit and within the committee’s power: pass the bill, amend a named section, or hold it.
Contact and availability. You are offering to follow up in writing.

The written statement is not a research paper. It is closer to a brief: footnoted, argumentative, and aimed at the decision in front of the committee.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
17.6 Anticipating questions
If a member asks you a question, a three-sentence answer is almost always the right length: the direct response, the evidence, and the connection back to your ask. Expect five types.
The “who are you” question. “Who funded this, and who asked you to do it?” Say who you are and whether anyone paid for the work, and say why the finding stands regardless.
The “overreach” question. “Isn’t this an unfunded mandate on every small town clerk?” Acknowledge the concern, point to the bill’s fiscal note if it has one, and point to the narrowest version of your ask.
The “wrong expert” question. “You’re a student, not a lawyer.” Concede the limit, name what your analysis does show, and name the legal sources you relied on.
The “already handled” question. “Doesn’t CORA already require a written denial?” Yes, for the requester. Explain that a denial sent to one person is not a pattern anyone else can see, and that the absence of an administrative appeal makes that pattern matter.
The “wrong level” question. “Shouldn’t each county decide this for itself?” Sometimes it should. Say which part belongs in state law (what CORA requires of every custodian) and which part a county can do on its own, as Boulder County’s archive shows.
The worst move is answering a question you were not asked. If you do not know, say so and offer to follow up in writing. The follow-up becomes part of the record too.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
17.7 Practice delivery and timing
Record yourself. Time it. Nearly every first draft runs long. The first cut is an adjective you did not know you wrote; the second is a paragraph you liked; the third is the transition you kept because it sounded smart. Print the statement, mark breaths in pencil, and underline the one phrase you must land. Reading from a printed page is fine. Reading from a phone that dims halfway through is not.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
17.8 Exercises
Exercise 17.1 (Guided). Read Haugen’s October 2021 Senate testimony. Mark every passage of personal voice, every empirical claim, and every specific ask. Count each category and write 200 words on what the ratios say about the genre.
Exercise 17.2 (Runnable, real public data). Choose an archived committee hearing on a bill from the General Assembly’s website, using the hearing’s archived audio. For every public witness, log start and end times, stated position, whether they made a specific ask, whether the ask was within the committee’s power, and whether they cited evidence. Load the log with pandas and report the median duration, the share of witnesses who exceeded the chair’s limit, and the share who made an actionable ask.
Exercise 17.3 (Guided). Draft three-sentence answers to the five question types above, tailored to your own ask. Read each aloud and confirm it fits in under twenty seconds.
Exercise 17.4 (Timing). Write a three-minute and a two-minute version of your oral statement, because chairs sometimes cut the clock when many witnesses sign up. Record at least three takes of each and log the durations in a CSV. Revise until every take of the three-minute version lands between 2:45 and 3:00.
Exercise 17.5 (Submittable artifact: testimony for a state legislative committee). Produce a testimony package with three parts:

Technical artifact. Tracker entries for the released records requests you chose (from Boulder County’s Public Records Archive or another custodian’s published releases), an extraction notebook that turns the released records into a table, and an exemptions and remedy ledger, delivered as a notebook or small repository someone else can clone and run.
Public text. Written testimony (about 1,000 words) and a recorded oral statement (about three minutes) on a named bill or interim-committee topic before a named committee of the Colorado General Assembly, with your position stated as you would enter it when you register.
Provenance, gaps, and AI-use note (about 300 words). Which pressure did you meet? Which installed-base elements (Chapter 2) did your artifact build, and which are still missing? State provenance and license and disclose how you used AI tools.

If the bill is heard while you are ready, register and testify, or submit the written statement through the legislature’s website before the hearing closes.

title: 17  Testimony
text:
17.9 Closing and what comes next
Most people testify a handful of times in their lives. For all of them, the habit of producing the paper trail matters more than the live performance: the written statement, the notebook, the ledger, and the follow-up email are what outlast the hearing.
Testimony has a written cousin with a longer clock. Chapter 18 takes it to the county, where planning decisions on land use dockets are made by a Planning Commission and a Board of County Commissioners that must take public comment, and then to the state and federal agencies that write rules. If your evidence concerns a system a federal agency uses, the report genre of Chapter 15 may reach a reader with more authority over it than any state committee.

title: 18  Public Comments
text:
18.1 How a county land use docket works
Counties decide what gets built where, and almost nobody you know has written them a comment about it. In unincorporated Boulder County, the Community Planning and Permitting department reviews land use applications under the Boulder County Comprehensive Plan and the county’s Land Use Code. A nine-member Planning Commission, appointed by the Board of County Commissioners, holds public hearings on many of those applications and on proposed changes to the code itself. For a few matters (the Comprehensive Plan and Location and Extent review) the Planning Commission decides; for everything else it recommends, and the Board of County Commissioners makes the binding decision at a later public hearing (Boulder County Land Use Department 2014; Boulder County, n.d.). At every step, anyone may comment in writing, cite the docket number, and have the comment made part of the public record. The door is open. Most of the profession walks past it.
A public comment is a written argument submitted to a body that must consider it before deciding, on that body’s schedule. It is the planning lineage’s genre. Planning (Chapter 9) asks who was in the room and whose knowledge counts as evidence; the comment period is its standing answer, a room anyone may enter, in writing, before a deadline. This chapter works at the county, where land use decisions are made and recorded. You will find a live docket in the county’s own data, read the referral for the criteria the decision turns on, compute evidence from county open data, and draft a comment that carries it. A final section takes the genre to the state and federal levels, where agencies writing rules must take written comment too.
Every application or code amendment gets a docket number. The prefix names the type and the middle digits the year: SU-25-0002 is a Special Use Review docket from 2025, DC-25-0003 a Land Use Code text amendment. Staff refer the docket to other agencies and to the public, collect comments, and write a staff report that evaluates the proposal against the criteria in the Land Use Code. The staff report is the document your comment has to answer, because it is the document the commissioners will read.
Timing matters more than at any other level of government. The county’s referral memo for docket DC-25-0003, a 2025 package of Land Use Code clarifications, told the public that comments received by a stated deadline would go into the Planning Commission’s staff packet, and that later comments would be shared with the commission and included in the packet for the Board of County Commissioners’ hearing. It also said, plainly, “All comments will be made part of the public record” (Boulder County Community Planning and Permitting 2025). The county’s published guidelines for Planning Commission hearings add three practical rules: public testimony is generally limited to three minutes per speaker, speakers present together may pool time up to ten minutes, and handouts or long documents given to staff at least eight days before the hearing can be included in the commissioners’ packets. They also say that the official record of a hearing is its audio recording (Boulder County Land Use Department 2014).
County comments are written, which suits data scientists. They are read, because they go into the commissioners’ packet. And they enter a record that outlasts the decision: years later, when someone asks why a parcel was rezoned, the docket file is where they look.

title: 18  Public Comments
section: 18.2 Why data scientists underuse this genre
text:
18.2 Why data scientists underuse this genre
Comments are lower-friction than testimony and higher-leverage than op-eds, and the profession submits shockingly few. Nobody invited you; the form is unfamiliar, since no county publishes a style guide for comments the way newspapers publish pitch guidelines; and the outcome is uncertain, because the commission may adopt your proposed condition, mention your comment in passing, or neither. A genre whose effect is cumulative feels unrewarding to a profession that likes metrics. It is, nonetheless, how much of the built environment gets shaped.

title: 18  Public Comments
text:
18.3 The substantive comment standard
Decision makers distinguish substantive comments from expressions of sentiment. A substantive comment identifies the specific provisions or criteria it responds to, offers evidence or analysis the staff report does not already contain, and proposes specific changes: a revised code sentence, a condition of approval, a request that staff supply a missing analysis before the hearing. A sentiment comment says the writer supports or opposes the proposal. A hundred letters of opposition tell the commissioners how a neighborhood feels; one substantive comment can change what the staff report says.
County land use has a wrinkle the federal process lacks. Decisions on individual applications are often treated as quasi-judicial: the commissioners act like judges applying the code’s criteria to evidence in the record, and contacts with them outside the hearing may be restricted. Code amendments, by contrast, are legislative.  Ask the docket planner which kind yours is. For a quasi-judicial docket, put everything in the written record and tie every claim to a criterion.






TipThe Missing Manual



Boulder County publishes its land use dockets as a public map layer, and the layer behaves like what it is: a view of a permitting database, not a dataset designed for you. Old docket numbers reappear with new application dates (a 1985 docket can show a 2026 date when the record is reopened), many records have no status, and the status vocabulary is long and inconsistent (“Closed,” “Closed Complete,” “Accepted Completed”). The server returns at most 1,000 records per request, so a broad query silently stops at 1,000 unless you page with resultOffset. The layer also carries owner names. You do not need them to write a comment, so do not request them: name the fields you want in outFields rather than asking for *. Finally, the county’s zoning layer includes each incorporated municipality as a single polygon with an X prefix (XBO for Boulder); county zoning does not apply there, so drop those polygons before computing anything about the unincorporated county.

title: 18  Public Comments
section: 18.4 Tutorial, part 1: finding a live docket
text:
18.4 Tutorial, part 1: finding a live docket
Community Planning and Permitting lists applications under review on its website and links them to a map. The same records are queryable through the county’s ArcGIS REST service, which means you can filter dockets by type and date without scraping.
import requests
import pandas as pd

ACCELA = ("https://maps.bouldercounty.org/arcgis/rest/services/"
          "PLANNING/OP_Accela_Poly/MapServer/0/query")
FIELDS = "CAPID,DocketType,ApplicationDate,ApplicationStatus,DocumentTitle,DocketLink"
HEARD = ["Special Use Review", "Rezoning", "Location and Extent Review",
         "Boulder County Comprehensive Plan Amendment"]

def dockets(since="2025-01-01"):
    types = ", ".join(f"'{t}'" for t in HEARD)
    params = {"where": f"DocketType IN ({types}) AND ApplicationDate >= DATE '{since}'",
              "outFields": FIELDS, "returnGeometry": "false",
              "orderByFields": "ApplicationDate DESC", "f": "json"}
    r = requests.get(ACCELA, params=params, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    df = pd.DataFrame([f["attributes"] for f in r.json()["features"]])
    df["ApplicationDate"] = pd.to_datetime(df["ApplicationDate"], unit="ms").dt.date
    return df

d = dockets()
print(len(d))
print(d[["CAPID", "ApplicationDate", "ApplicationStatus"]].head(4).to_string(index=False))
# => 12
# =>      CAPID ApplicationDate ApplicationStatus
# => SU-26-0003      2026-04-28        Incomplete
# => SU-26-0002      2026-03-10        Incomplete
# => SU-85-0023      2026-03-05              None
# => LE-90-0008      2026-02-25              None
# (as of October 2026; results change as dockets move)
The HEARD list picks docket types that usually go to a public hearing. Each DocketLink opens the docket page, with the referral packet, staff report, and hearing dates. Code amendment (DC) dockets are listed separately on the county’s Land Use Code update page.

title: 18  Public Comments
section: 18.5 Tutorial, part 2: evidence for a code amendment
text:
18.5 Tutorial, part 2: evidence for a code amendment
Take DC-25-0003 as a worked example. Its referral packet proposed, among other things, new text for parking standards in three zoning districts: Transitional (T), Multiple Family (MF), and Niwot Rural Community District I (NRCD I) (Boulder County Community Planning and Permitting 2025). Its referral period closed in December 2025, so treat it as practice.  A reader of the packet would want to know a simple thing the packet does not say: how much of the county does the parking change touch? The county’s open zoning and parcel layers answer it.
import geopandas as gpd

BASE = "https://maps.bouldercounty.org/arcgis/rest/services/"
ZONING = BASE + "PLANNING/LUC_ZoningDistricts/MapServer/0/query"
PARCELS = BASE + "Emap/BOCO_Parcels/MapServer/0/query"

def layer(url, **params):
    params = {"outSR": 4326, "f": "geojson", **params}
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame.from_features(r.json()["features"], crs="EPSG:4326")

zones = layer(ZONING, where="ZONECLASS IN ('T','MF','NRCD1')",
              outFields="ZONECLASS,ZONEDESC").to_crs("EPSG:26913")
zones["acres"] = zones.area / 4046.8564224          # UTM 13N, meters
print(zones.groupby("ZONECLASS").agg(polygons=("acres", "size"),
                                     acres=("acres", "sum")).round(1))
# =>            polygons  acres
# => ZONECLASS
# => MF                7  234.6
# => NRCD1             1   10.1
# => T                 7   50.4
About 295 acres, roughly 0.07 percent of the unincorporated county’s zoned area. The parcel count tells a different story:
frames = []
for geom in zones.to_crs(4326).geometry:   # one box per polygon; each stays under the 5,000-record cap
    x0, y0, x1, y1 = geom.bounds
    frames.append(layer(PARCELS, where="1=1", outFields="PARCEL_NO",
                        geometry=f"{x0},{y0},{x1},{y1}",
                        geometryType="esriGeometryEnvelope", inSR=4326))
parcels = pd.concat(frames).drop_duplicates("PARCEL_NO").to_crs("EPSG:26913")
parcels["geometry"] = parcels.representative_point()
inside = gpd.sjoin(parcels, zones[["ZONECLASS", "geometry"]], predicate="within")
print(inside.groupby("ZONECLASS")["PARCEL_NO"].nunique().to_dict())
# => {'MF': 1626, 'NRCD1': 27, 'T': 155}
A tiny share of the land, but about 1,800 parcels, most in multifamily districts where condominium units are often separate parcels. That finding neither supports nor opposes the amendment, but it tells the commission whom the amendment affects, and it suggests a request (map the districts in the packet; notify the affected owners and residents) the county could grant without changing a word of the proposal.

title: 18  Public Comments
section: 18.6 The shape of a substantive county comment
text:
18.6 The shape of a substantive county comment
A county comment has a header, an introduction, a body organized by the criteria or code sections at issue, and a conclusion listing specific requests.
[Name, address or affiliation, contact]          [Date]

To: Community Planning and Permitting, [docket planner]
Re: Docket [DC-25-0003], [title]
    Comment for the [Planning Commission / Board of County Commissioners] packet
The introduction says who you are, which sections of the proposal you address, and your position in a paragraph. The body answers the criteria:
Proposed parking standards for the T, MF, and NRCD I districts (Appendix A)

The referral packet does not state how many properties the change affects.
Using the county's zoning and parcel layers (Exhibit A, with code), I
count about 1,800 parcels within these districts, 1,626 of them in MF
districts. I ask that the staff report include a map of the affected
districts and that notice of the hearing reach owners and residents of
these parcels.
That paragraph names the section, adds evidence the packet lacked, shows its method, and makes a request staff could adopt as written. Attach the exhibits (the CSV, the map, the notebook), send it before the packet deadline, and if you can, speak at the hearing, pointing to the written comment rather than reading it.

title: 18  Public Comments
text:
18.7 Tracking the docket
A docket accumulates documents over months: referral, staff report, recommendation, resolution. The SQLite tracker for records requests in Chapter 7 extends naturally with one table that serves every level of government.
import sqlite3

SCHEMA = """
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS dockets (
    docket_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,           -- 'DC-25-0003', 'FTC-2022-0053'
    level TEXT CHECK (level IN ('county','state','federal')),
    body TEXT NOT NULL, title TEXT NOT NULL,
    comment_deadline TEXT, hearing_date TEXT,
    status TEXT CHECK (status IN ('open','closed','decided','withdrawn')),
    my_comment_url TEXT);
"""
with sqlite3.connect("docket_tracker.sqlite") as conn:
    conn.executescript(SCHEMA)
A weekly job that flags dockets whose comment deadline falls within fourteen days will keep you from the most common first-time failure: missing the packet.






NoteIn the Public Interest



A county comment is ownership in procedural form. Chapter 5 defines ownership as collective, accountable governance over how public-relevant data and decisions are kept and used, and Chapter 9 shows how planning gave participation procedural teeth. A comment that enters the docket file is the public asserting a stake in a decision it does not control, in a record the county must keep. It is also oversight at the smallest scale, because your comment is now in the record the decision must rest on. The specific claim of this chapter is that a comment advances these values only when it adds checkable evidence about the criteria the decision turns on. A comment that reads as sentiment is participation of the kind Arnstein (1969) placed on the lower rungs: heard, counted, and set aside. Write it so it reads well out of context years from now, because that is when someone opening the docket file may need it.

title: 18  Public Comments
section: 18.8 Commenting at the state and federal levels
text:
18.8 Commenting at the state and federal levels
The genre works the same way above the county, with longer documents and more formal rules. In Colorado, the State Administrative Procedure Act requires an agency proposing a rule to publish notice in the Colorado Register and give the public an opportunity to submit written comments and to be heard.  Check the Register when a technology law you care about passes; rulemaking is where it becomes operational.
At the federal level, the Administrative Procedure Act’s rulemaking section, 5 U.S.C. § 553, requires an agency proposing a substantive rule to publish notice in the Federal Register, give the public an opportunity to participate “through submission of written data, views, or arguments,” and consider what it receives (US Congress 1946). Substantive comments become part of the administrative record a court examines if the rule is challenged, and courts look for an agency’s engagement with substantive comments, not a response to each copy of a campaign letter (Congressional Research Service 2023). Agencies treat identical comments as one comment with many signatories, and the Federal Communications Commission’s 2017 net neutrality docket showed that floods can be faked: millions of its comments were filed under fabricated or stolen identities.  In 2025 the White House directed agencies to lean on the “good cause” exception when repealing rules, which skips comment altogether. 
For data scientists, the most useful federal dockets are often Paperwork Reduction Act notices. An agency that wants to start, change, or renew a collection of information from the public (a survey, a reporting form, the required fields of a federal data system) must publish a notice and invite comment, first for 60 days and then for 30 while the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs reviews it. The notices ask the same four questions every time: whether the collection is necessary and has practical utility, whether the burden estimate is accurate, how to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information, and how to minimize the burden on respondents. “Practical utility” is where an erosion audit (Chapter 5) shows who depends on a dataset an agency proposes to cut; “minimize the burden” is where a refusal specification (Chapter 13) argues a field should not be collected at all.
Regulations.gov, the shared federal docket system, has an API through api.data.gov with a free key (US General Services Administration 2024). Document search, docket retrieval, and comment retrieval are separate endpoints; submission uses a separate key, and for a single comment the web form is simpler.
import os

API_KEY = os.environ["REGULATIONS_GOV_API_KEY"]
BASE = "https://api.regulations.gov/v4"
HEADERS = {"X-Api-Key": API_KEY}

def open_documents(keyword, doc_type="Proposed Rule", after="2027-04-01"):
    params = {"filter[searchTerm]": keyword,
              "filter[documentType]": doc_type,      # or "Notice" for PRA notices
              "filter[commentEndDate][ge]": after,    # still open on this date
              "page[size]": 25, "sort": "-postedDate"}
    r = requests.get(f"{BASE}/documents", headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=30)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["data"]

for h in open_documents("information collection", doc_type="Notice")[:5]:
    a = h["attributes"]
    print(a["docketId"], a.get("commentEndDate"), a["title"][:60])
# (results depend on the day you run it)
The API has changed versions and authentication more than once; confirm the current version before writing code. A federal comment has the same shape as a county one, with the Federal Register citation in the header and the body organized by the notice’s numbered questions. The Federal Trade Commission’s 2022 commercial surveillance docket (FTC-2022-0053) holds good academic comments to read as templates.

title: 18  Public Comments
text:
18.9 Exercises
Exercise 18.1 (Guided; laptop, real data). Run dockets() with today’s date range. Pick three dockets that are open or scheduled for a hearing, open each DocketLink, and record the docket ID, type, status, referral or comment deadline, and hearing dates in docket_tracker.sqlite. Note one record whose status or date in the map layer disagrees with the docket page.
Exercise 18.2 (Guided). For one docket, read the referral packet or staff report and list every criterion or code section the decision turns on. For each, write one sentence naming the evidence that would bear on it and whether county open data could supply it.
Exercise 18.3 (Runnable, real public data). Compute one piece of evidence for your docket from the county’s open data layers: affected parcels, acreage by district, distance to a resource the Comprehensive Plan protects, or another measure tied to a criterion from 18.2. Save the notebook and a CSV exhibit, and write two sentences on the measure’s limits.
Exercise 18.4 (Other levels). Use open_documents() or the Colorado Register to find an open state or federal docket related to a dataset you have used. List the questions it asks, and classify three comments already filed there (or on a closed docket at the same agency) as substantive, sentiment, or off-topic, justifying each in 150 words.
Exercise 18.5 (Submittable artifact: a public comment on a live matter). Produce a comment package with three parts:

Technical artifact. The notebook and exhibits from 18.3 (or equivalent evidence for a state or federal docket), as a repository someone else can clone and run, with a provenance file for every layer or dataset used.
Public text. A substantive comment on a live Boulder County land use docket (or, if none fits your evidence, a live state or federal docket), ready to submit: docket number in the header, the criteria or sections you address, evidence attached as exhibits, and concrete requested changes.
Provenance, gaps, and AI-use note (about 300 words). Which pressure did you meet? Which installed-base elements (Chapter 2) did your artifact build, and which are still missing? State provenance and license and disclose how you used AI tools.

A submitted comment enters a permanent public record under your name. Submit it before the packet deadline if you stand behind it, keep the confirmation, and record the docket URL in your tracker.

title: 18  Public Comments
text:
18.10 Looking ahead
A comment is written for a decision about to be made. Chapter 19 writes for readers who come after the decision: it shows how to deposit your evidence, exhibits, and comment with a DOI, so the record you contributed to does not depend on a county website or a federal portal staying where it is. If your comment surfaced a question the docket could not answer, Chapter 16 shows how to ask someone to pay for the answer.

text:
