title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.1 Archives and climate, archives and memory
Every other genre in Part IV addresses an audience that already exists. An op-ed (Chapter 14) argues to a city reader holding tomorrow’s paper. A report (Chapter 15) answers a federal body that can act on it. A proposal (Chapter 16) speaks to reviewers convened this fiscal year. Testimony (Chapter 17) addresses a state legislative committee with a bill on its calendar. A public comment (Chapter 18) reaches a county planning commission before its packet deadline. Each of those publics is reachable because each is alive.
An archival deposit is different. You are contributing to a conversation with a public that does not yet exist. A graduate student in 2048 reading old EPA Toxics Release Inventory data to reconstruct an environmental-justice claim. A city staffer in 2035 looking for Colorado groundwater trends that a federal agency has since stopped publishing. A journalist in 2060 writing a retrospective on federal climate portals reorganized during this decade. None of those readers can be pitched to, invited, or surveyed. They will find what you deposited if, and only if, it is still there.
That is why the deposit is a genre of its own, and why it belongs at the end of any project in this book. You take the technical artifact and public text from any of the other genres, document them, and archive them in a repository that mints a Digital Object Identifier (DOI). Zenodo is this chapter’s deposit of record, because a DOI is what lets a future reader cite and resolve your work; an Internet Archive item is an optional mirror, valuable as a second copy but not a substitute for the DOI. The deposit is where openness, oversight, and ownership (Chapter 3, Chapter 4, Chapter 5) come to rest in a single physical-digital object: a bitstream, a checksum, a resolvable identifier, a provenance record, held by an institution committed to keeping them. This chapter teaches the workflow on a federal dataset at risk, the kind of record whose erosion Chapter 5 audits, and then applies it to your own work.
It is tempting to treat archival deposit as an afterthought. The archival profession has been saying for a decade that this is wrong. Tansey (2015) argues that climate change is an archival problem because the floods, fires, and storms that threaten records are the events that make those records most urgently needed. Mazurczyk and colleagues (2018) extend the argument quantitatively, mapping American archives against projected sea-level rise and showing how much institutional memory sits in places the country’s institutions are not planning to protect. Blanke (2024) takes it digital: the Anthropocene is also a problem for server rooms, for migrations across storage media, and for the economics of keeping bits online for a century.
Bluntly: the federal agencies whose datasets document the climate crisis are the same agencies whose data-retention budgets are most exposed to it. An EPA dataset is at risk from two directions. The weather can take the building. A single administration can take the dataset. The archive hedges both.
Ghaddar (2016) and Robinson-Sweet (2018) describe a second horizon: truth-and-reconciliation futures in which publics will want to examine what present governments recorded, classified, suppressed, or destroyed. What you deposit, and what you decline to deposit, is part of what a later public can say about us. Someone will go looking. Either your work is there or it is not.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.2 The institutional landscape
A “durable” archive is not a synonym for “a server you rent.” Durability is an institutional property: a mandate to preserve, a budget funded across political cycles, a succession plan, and federated backup so the loss of one building does not destroy the collection. A handful of institutions meet that standard. Several more claim to and do not.
The Internet Archive operates the Wayback Machine and a general items repository (Internet Archive 2024). It accepts almost anything, mints durable URLs (not DOIs), and exposes a Python client. That makes it a fine mirror, not a deposit of record for work you want cited. Its repeated court battles are a sign of how much it matters.
Zenodo, operated by CERN, accepts datasets, code, and papers up to 50GB, mints a DOI on publication, and preserves what it holds on CERN’s long-term infrastructure (CERN 2024). A Zenodo DOI is the shortest path from a laptop to a citable identifier, which is why it is this chapter’s deposit of record.
Figshare and OSF play similar roles (Center for Open Science 2024). ICPSR is the standard for social-science survey data and restricted-use materials (Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research 2024); Dryad serves the life sciences (Dryad 2024); Dataverse is a federated platform at dozens of universities.
Software Heritage archives source code at scale (Software Heritage 2024). LOCKSS (“Lots of Copies Keep Stuff Safe”) is the federated-preservation backbone used by libraries (Stanford University Libraries 2024). Perma.cc captures web pages for legal citation (Harvard Library Innovation Lab 2024). EDGI coordinates volunteer archiving of federal environmental data at risk of removal (Environmental Data and Governance Initiative 2024).
Notice what is not on this list. GitHub, Hugging Face, Google Drive, Dropbox, S3, and personal websites are not preservation institutions; their retention guarantees are product roadmaps, not mandates. They can be links in a preservation chain, never the last link. If the only copy of your dataset lives on a platform whose survival depends on next quarter’s earnings, it is not archived. It is stored.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.3 Federated archiving as political strategy
That list is also a political arrangement. LOCKSS’s founding claim is in its name: safety comes from redundancy across independent custodians (Stanford University Libraries 2024). When the EPA’s climate pages were reorganized in 2017, EDGI’s volunteer “data rescue” events moved copies of at-risk datasets into Internet Archive items before the changes took effect. No single institution was going to do that; a federation did.
An archival deposit is therefore political as well as technical. Depositing the same dataset in two independent repositories, in two jurisdictions, hedges against any one failing, being captured, or being compelled. A citation needs a DOI, so Zenodo is the deposit of record; an Internet Archive mirror is optional and recommended. That redundancy is not theater; it is the minimum viable federation.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
section: 19.4 The running example: EPA Toxics Release Inventory
text:
19.4 The running example: EPA Toxics Release Inventory
The Toxics Release Inventory (TRI), mandated by the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act of 1986, collects annual self-reports from industrial facilities on releases of listed toxic chemicals to air, water, and land (US Environmental Protection Agency 2024). It is one of the most-cited environmental-justice datasets in the United States and has run continuously since 1987. Like every federal environmental dataset, it is subject to threshold changes, definitional revisions, and occasional quiet removal of historical files when schemas are updated.
Pick a TRI reporting year’s facility-level file (the 2022 Basic Data File is small enough for a laptop), download it, keep the original bytes. The workflow below transfers to any at-risk federal environmental dataset: NOAA Climate Data Online, USGS groundwater, EPA AirData, NOAA GHCN-D.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.5 Preservation-appropriate formats
Before any upload, convert your artifacts into formats still readable in fifty years. This is the highest-leverage decision in the workflow. The Library of Congress’s “Sustainability of Digital Formats” registry rates formats on openness, adoption, transparency, and self-documentation (Library of Congress 2024). The short version:

Tabular data: CSV (UTF-8, RFC 4180) as primary; Parquet as companion for large tables. Not Excel; its binary format is semi-proprietary and its date handling is notorious.
Documentation: plain text or Markdown. Not Word. A .docx opened in 2045 will render in ways neither you nor your reader can predict.
Images: TIFF or PNG. Not JPEG; every re-save degrades it.
Geospatial: GeoJSON or GeoPackage primary; Shapefile as companion (its 10-character field-name limit truncates columns).
Code: plain-text source files, not notebooks, with an HTML export attached. A .py is more likely to parse in 2050 than an .ipynb.

You will work harder than you want on this step. Do it anyway.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
section: 19.6 Mirroring with the Internet Archive client
text:
19.6 Mirroring with the Internet Archive client
The mirror is optional. If you make one, make it first, so the DOI record can point to it. The internetarchive Python client and its ia command-line companion are the fastest way to make one (Internet Archive 2024). Run ia configure once to store your credentials, then upload. The item identifier is a short unique string that becomes part of the URL (https://archive.org/details/<identifier>). Identifiers are forever; choose one that describes the content.
from internetarchive import upload, get_item

metadata = {
    "title": "EPA Toxics Release Inventory, 2022 Basic Data File (mirror)",
    "creator": "Your Name, Your Institution",
    "date": "2027-04-23",
    "subject": ["environment", "toxics", "EPA", "TRI",
                "environmental justice"],
    "language": "eng",
    "licenseurl": "https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/",
    "description": (
        "Mirror of the US EPA Toxics Release Inventory 2022 Basic "
        "Data File, retrieved from epa.gov on 2027-04-20. See the "
        "attached preservation plan."
    ),
    "mediatype": "data",
    "collection": "opensource",
}

files = ["tri_2022_us.csv", "tri_2022_us.parquet",
         "datasheet.md", "README.md", "LICENSE.txt",
         "preservation_plan.md"]

upload("epa-tri-2022-basic-mirror", files=files, metadata=metadata)
# => [<Response [200]>, <Response [200]>, ...] on success

# Verify the deposit. Compare server SHA-1 to what you computed locally.
item = get_item("epa-tri-2022-basic-mirror")
for f in item.files:
    print(f["name"], f["size"], f.get("sha1"))
HTTP 200 does not guarantee the files are actually there. Fetch the item back and confirm each file has non-zero size and a matching SHA-1. That verification is what most tutorials skip.






TipThe Missing Manual



The internetarchive client returns success codes on uploads that silently failed: the item is created, the files are listed with size 0, and the HTTP layer looks fine. Always verify by fetching the item back with ia metadata <item_id> or get_item(id) and comparing the server’s SHA-1 to yours. Separately, Zenodo DOIs take up to an hour to resolve after minting; do not panic when a fresh DOI returns “not found” ten seconds after publishing. The other silent killer is format choice. The difference between a file that survives fifty years and one that does not is usually not storage redundancy but format: CSV beats Excel, TIFF beats JPEG, Markdown beats Word, plain source beats a bundled notebook. Storage is easy. Legibility is hard.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.7 Minting a DOI with Zenodo
Zenodo’s REST API issues a DOI on publication, which is what makes it the deposit of record in the federated pair (CERN 2024). Request a personal access token from zenodo.org/account/settings/applications/, scope it to deposit:write and deposit:actions, and treat it like a password.
import os, requests

ZENODO = "https://zenodo.org/api"
PARAMS = {"access_token": os.environ["ZENODO_TOKEN"]}
HEADERS = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}

# 1. Create an empty deposition.
r = requests.post(f"{ZENODO}/deposit/depositions",
                  params=PARAMS, headers=HEADERS, json={})
r.raise_for_status()
dep = r.json()

# 2. Upload files into the deposition bucket.
for path in ["tri_2022_us.csv", "tri_2022_us.parquet",
             "datasheet.md", "README.md", "preservation_plan.md"]:
    with open(path, "rb") as fh:
        requests.put(f"{dep['links']['bucket']}/{os.path.basename(path)}",
                     data=fh, params=PARAMS).raise_for_status()

# 3. Attach Dublin Core metadata.
meta = {"metadata": {
    "title": "EPA Toxics Release Inventory, 2022 Basic Data File (mirror)",
    "upload_type": "dataset",
    "description": "Mirror of the US EPA TRI 2022 Basic Data File...",
    "creators": [{"name": "Your Name",
                  "affiliation": "Your Institution"}],
    "keywords": ["environment", "toxics", "EPA", "TRI",
                 "environmental justice", "at-risk data"],
    "license": "cc-zero", "language": "eng",
    "related_identifiers": [  # drop the first entry if you made no mirror
        {"identifier": "https://archive.org/details/epa-tri-2022-basic-mirror",
         "relation": "isIdenticalTo", "resource_type": "dataset"},
        {"identifier": "https://www.epa.gov/toxics-release-inventory-tri-program",
         "relation": "isDerivedFrom", "resource_type": "other"},
    ],
}}
requests.put(f"{ZENODO}/deposit/depositions/{dep['id']}",
             params=PARAMS, headers=HEADERS, json=meta).raise_for_status()

# 4. Publish. This mints the DOI and makes the record immutable.
r = requests.post(
    f"{ZENODO}/deposit/depositions/{dep['id']}/actions/publish",
    params=PARAMS)
print(r.json()["doi"])  # the API returns your record's DOI here, e.g. 10.5281/zenodo.7654321
The related_identifiers field is where federation becomes legible. You are telling Zenodo that its record is identical to the Internet Archive item and derived from the EPA source. A future user landing on any of the three can follow the chain to the others. Before going live, test against sandbox.zenodo.org: the API is identical, the DOIs are not real, the mistakes are free.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.8 A preservation plan
A deposit without a preservation plan is a bet that someone else will figure out what you meant. A plan makes the bet explicit by answering four questions.
Retention. How long do you intend the deposit to remain accessible, and under what conditions would it be withdrawn? “Indefinite, absent legal compulsion” is acceptable. So is “Ten years, then re-evaluate.” Specify something.
Migration. What happens when the format becomes unreadable? Parquet in 2027 will not be Parquet in 2057. State whether migration is the depositor’s responsibility (usually yes for the first generation), the repository’s (sometimes yes for major archives), or unresolved. Name a review interval; five years is reasonable.
Custodianship. Who is responsible when you move, change institutions, or leave the work? Karasti and Blomberg (2018) call this “maintenance across decades,” and their infrastructure studies (Chapter 2) is the backbone of the answer. Designate a successor, an institution, or a community. “My GitHub account” is not an answer. “The University of Colorado Boulder libraries’ digital preservation program, with EDGI as federated redundancy” is.
Access and refusal. Tie back to the tiered-access matrix from Chapter 5. Open access or tiered (DUA, embargo windows)? Refusal conditions from Chapter 13 under which portions should be withdrawn? Make the rules legible before a future dispute requires them.
A plan that answers those four questions, committed alongside the dataset in the same deposit, is a preservation plan and a governance document. Someone will need it.






NoteIn the Public Interest



The public interest includes people who do not yet exist. That is not a metaphor. The graduate student in 2048, the council staffer in 2035, the journalist in 2060: they are the public your deposit serves, and the archive is how you speak to them. This is the chapter where the book’s three values come to rest. Openness (Chapter 3) lets future readers find the bits, read them, and cite them. Oversight (Chapter 4) lets them hold present institutions accountable using records the institutions did not destroy. Ownership (Chapter 5) binds the deposit to a custodianship chain that does not evaporate with a funding cycle. The installed base (Chapter 2) was never only about the present; it was always about whether the future could read us.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
section: 19.9 Assembling a deposit of your own work
text:
19.9 Assembling a deposit of your own work
The TRI deposit is practice. The deposit that counts is your own work, and if you have finished another chapter in Part IV, most of its parts exist. The technical artifact, exported to plain-source .py files with an HTML rendering, is the core. The public text (the op-ed, report section, proposal, testimony, or comment) sits beside it as Markdown, with the version you submitted and, if it was published or entered into a record, a link to that copy. Your note on provenance, gaps, and AI use becomes the README’s provenance section, and a datasheet in the form Chapter 5 describes documents any data you collected. The preservation plan described above carries any tiered-access decisions (Chapter 5) and refusal conditions (Chapter 13). A short account of the work’s limits, of the kind Chapter 20 asks for, goes in too, so a future reader meets it alongside the work.
If you produced artifacts in several genres, deposit each as its own record and gather them in a Zenodo community, so each can be cited separately and found together.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.10 Verifying and citing
A deposit that cannot be cited is a backup. A deposit that can be cited is a contribution. After publication, resolve the DOI and confirm it lands. If you made a mirror, paste the Internet Archive URL into a fresh logged-out session and confirm you can download the files. Compute their SHA-256 and compare to what you deposited. Then write the citation, substituting your minted DOI for the XXXXXXX placeholder, in the form your future readers will paste:

Your Name (2027). EPA Toxics Release Inventory, 2022 Basic Data File (mirror) [Dataset]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXX. Also at Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/epa-tri-2022-basic-mirror.

That citation is the shortest route from “I did the work” to “here is the permanent link,” the minimum unit of the public-interest infrastructure Keegan (2026) describes. Write it.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.11 Exercises
Exercise 19.1 (Guided, optional mirror). Install the internetarchive client and register at archive.org. Pick an at-risk federal environmental dataset; the endangered resource you named at the end of Chapter 5 is a natural choice, as is EPA TRI 2022, a NOAA Climate Data Online file, or a USGS groundwater extract. Download it, convert to CSV and Parquet, write a one-page datasheet following Chapter 5, and deposit the bundle as an Internet Archive item with full Dublin Core metadata. Verify with ia metadata <item_id> that every file has non-zero size and a matching SHA-1. Record the item URL and the verification output.
Exercise 19.2 (Guided). Create a Zenodo account, request an access token, and test the deposit flow against sandbox.zenodo.org before going live. Then deposit the dataset bundle to production Zenodo, with related_identifiers entries for the source and, if you made one, your Internet Archive mirror. Verify the DOI resolves (allow up to an hour). Record the DOI, the resolved URL, and how long resolution took.
Exercise 19.3 (Reflective). Write a two-to-three-page preservation plan for the dataset. Address retention, migration, custodianship, and access and refusal (tying back to Chapter 5 and Chapter 13). Reuse the sustainability plan from the last exercise of Chapter 11 as the custodianship spine. Commit the plan into the deposit as preservation_plan.md and update the metadata to reference it.
Exercise 19.4 (Open-ended). Propose a public-interest data infrastructure that should exist in 2035 but does not: a federated archive of state benefits-administration audit logs, a repository of municipal algorithmic impact assessments, a climate-resilient mirror of at-risk federal datasets. In three to five pages, say what it is, whom it serves, what its first five years look like, how its outputs would be deposited, and who bears the maintenance labor across decades.
Exercise 19.5 (Submittable artifact: a deposit with a DOI). Deposit your own work, with three parts:

Technical artifact. The runnable artifact from another Part IV chapter (or from any tutorial in this book you extended), in preservation formats, with a README someone else can follow to rerun it.
Public text. The public text that artifact supported, as Markdown, with a link to the submitted or published version if one exists, plus Dublin Core metadata and a citation written for a reader in 2050.
Provenance, gaps, and AI-use note with a datasheet and the preservation plan from 19.3, covering retention, migration, custodianship, and access.

Publish the record on Zenodo (or another repository that mints a DOI) so that it receives one; an Internet Archive identifier alone does not meet this standard, though a cross-linked mirror is welcome. Verify the files, resolve the DOI from a logged-out browser, and add the citation to your CV or project page.

title: 19  Archival Deposits
text:
19.12 Closing
A deposit is a promise to a reader you will never meet, and a promise needs an honest account of its limits. That is why the account of limits travels inside the deposit. The last chapter, Chapter 20, turns the book’s framework on itself: whose records it prefers, whose refusals it postpones, and which levels of government it assumes will be there to read what you archived.

text:
19.13 Further Reading and Resources

Library of Congress, Sustainability of Digital Formats: https://www.loc.gov/preservation/digital/formats/. The registry that tells you, for any format, how scared to be about using it.

title: Closing
text:
Why close with limits
The book has one framework, and it has used it on almost everything. Part I named three pressures on public knowledge (enclosure, exemption, and erosion), paired each with the value that answers it (openness, oversight, and ownership), and described the installed base that makes those values last. Part II borrowed methods from five professions. Part III mapped the adjacent conversations that build, deliver, and contest data systems. Part IV turned all of it into genres addressed to bodies that can act: an op-ed to a city, a public comment to a county, testimony to a state legislature, a report to a federal agency, a proposal to a funder, and a deposit to whoever comes next.
This last part has a single chapter and a different job. It does not add a lineage, a level of government, or a pressure. It asks where the framework stops working.
Keegan (2026) anticipates five critiques of the framework (the realist, the critical, the libertarian, the positivist, and the pessimist) and answers each by specifying more infrastructure. That conversion is the framework’s strength, and it is also a bias: a critique that cannot be answered with an identifier, a retention rule, or an escalation pathway has nowhere to land. The book’s introduction admits several partialities of its own. It is US-centric. It is more comfortable with records than with refusal. It is thin on the labor that keeps records alive and on whether the records measure what they claim. Admissions like these are easy to make and rarely checked.
20  The Limits of the Framework checks them. It sets out the five critiques, then seven limits the framework does not resolve, from US-centrism to the way its four levels of government presume functioning institutions at each one. It then borrows the method of the audit chapters and applies it to the book itself: a reflexive audit that codes the book’s own cases by region, level of government, pressure, value, remedy, and fit, and counts where refusal appears and where the taxonomy strains. The chapter closes with a critical-reflection memo you write about your own work, asking whose interests it serves, who was not consulted, and where the framework failed for your case.

title: Closing
text:
How to read it
You can read 20  The Limits of the Framework first. A skeptical reader may prefer to, since it states plainly what the rest of the book takes for granted. Its tutorial needs only pandas and an inline table, and each limit links to the chapters whose cases it questions. Read last, it works as an audit of everything before it. Read first, it is a list of things to watch for. Either way, the book’s last instruction is to recode the cases you disagree with, and to send the revision back.






Keegan, Brian C. 2026. “Public Interest Data Infrastructuring.” Under Review.

title: 20  The Limits of the Framework
text:
20.1 Five critiques the framework anticipates
For nineteen chapters this book has used one framework as a diagnostic. Three pressures (enclosure, exemption, erosion) narrow what the public can observe; three values (openness, oversight, ownership) push back; an installed base of identifiers, records, access tiers, retention rules, and escalation pathways makes those values last. The worked examples applied it at four levels of government: a city’s council and campaign finance records, a county’s land use dockets and records archive, a state’s open records statute and AI law, and the nation’s AI inventories and vanishing datasets. This closing chapter does the thing every good audit eventually does: it points the instrument at itself.
A framework that cannot name where it fails is not a framework; it is a brand. Keegan (2026) anticipates five critiques and treats each as a design constraint on the installed base rather than an attack to deflect. But a framework’s author is the person least able to see what it cannot see. The book’s introduction lists five ways it is partial: US-centric, comfortable with records and less comfortable with refusal, thin on labor, thin on measurement theory, and over-reliant on professional lineages. Those admissions are honest. They are also unaudited.
The question is therefore empirical as well as conceptual: where, in the cases this book actually uses, does the framework bind? By the end you will have coded the book’s own cases, counted them, and written a critical-reflection memo on a piece of your own work.
Keegan (2026) names five objections and answers each with installed-base requirements.
The realist says the open-data era is over. The framework accepts the description and rejects the fatalism: if voluntary access is gone, openness becomes a retention and reference problem (redundant repositories, persistent identifiers, statutory access rights). Chapter 19 is the realist’s answer in miniature.
The critical objection asks how this differs from data for good, civic tech, and responsible AI (the conversations mapped in Chapter 11). The answer is a testable design stance: a project that cannot specify identifiers, provenance, retention, access tiers, and escalation pathways is probably another pilot that will not survive enclosure and erosion.
The libertarian says oversight will kill innovation. The framework replies that standardized logging, versioning, and audit interfaces can reduce friction by making expectations predictable.
The positivist says data science should not be political. The framework answers procedurally: documented assumptions and reproducible outputs are what rigor already demands. Green (2021) makes the stronger reply, that data science is already political action whether or not its practitioners say so.
The pessimist says these systems are too complex to oversee. The framework answers with “auditable complexity”: change logs, provenance, retention, and role-based access for specialized intermediaries.
Notice the shape: each critique becomes a requirement for more infrastructure. That conversion is the framework’s strength and its signature bias. A critique that cannot be answered with an installed-base element has nowhere to land.
crumbs: 20  The Limits of the Framework

title: 20  The Limits of the Framework
section: 20.2 Seven limits the framework does not resolve
text:
20.2 Seven limits the framework does not resolve
These limits are not bugs to patch; they are where the framework’s assumptions show.

20.2.1 US-centrism
The book’s legal machinery is American: FOIA, CORA, the Administrative Procedure Act, the CFAA, NYC Local Law 144. Non-US cases appear mostly as counter-cases, one or two per chapter, which is better than none and worse than parity. A counter-case is defined by what it counters: SyRI (District Court of The Hague 2020) enters the book as a test of oversight, not as the center of a Dutch administrative-law tradition. Taylor (2019) calls for data justice framed globally rather than from one country outward. This book frames from one country outward.


20.2.2 Records over refusal
The installed base takes linkability, durable identifiers, and retention as load-bearing. Chapter 13 takes refusal seriously, drawing on Zong and Matias (2024), D’Ignazio and Klein (2020), Garcia et al. (2022), Carroll et al. (2020), and Te Mana Raraunga (Te Mana Raraunga 2018). But the framework’s own discussion section concedes the problem: identifiers “can intensify surveillance and cross-system targeting,” and retention “can preserve harmful traces indefinitely” (Keegan 2026). Its proposed fix is “minimum viable safeguards” (access tiers, minimization, accountable intermediaries). That is still a records-first answer. Starting from refusal and arriving at records is a different book.


20.2.3 The labor inside data work
Someone transcribes the minutes, labels the training data, answers the CORA request, and keeps the checksums current. Gray and Suri (2019) documents the hidden workforce behind automated systems; Jarrahi et al. (2021) describes how algorithmic management reorganizes work around data. Keegan’s research agenda names “the labor of custodians, clerks, librarians, compliance officers, community archivists, and worker organizers who keep evidence alive” (Keegan 2026), and Chapter 10 meets worker observatories and worker-built tools for auditing algorithmic management (Calacci and Pentland 2022). Yet the six installed-base elements contain no element for who does the work, under what conditions, and for what pay. Maintenance appears as continuity, a property of records, rather than as a relation between people.


20.2.4 The state as partner and threat
The framework’s escalation pathways run through public institutions: courts, inspectors general, regulators, records offices. The book needs the state to be a partner. The book’s own cases show the state as a threat: SyRI and the Dutch childcare-benefits scandal (Amnesty International 2021), the Allegheny screening tool (Eubanks 2018), the LAPD programs that the Stop LAPD Spying Coalition refused (Stop LAPD Spying Coalition and Free Radicals 2020), and the federal dataset removals of Chapter 5. Levy and Johns (2016) show how transparency itself can be weaponized: demands for “open data” have been used to exclude inconvenient science from rulemaking. An installed base built to serve oversight can be captured to serve the overseen.


20.2.5 The measurement problem
The installed base makes records durable, not valid. A disaggregated audit in Chapter 8 reports error rates by group, but the groups are census categories, the outcome is a proxy, and the threshold is a policy choice. Selbst et al. (2019) call this the family of “abstraction traps”; Bowker and Star (2000) showed decades ago that classification systems encode the politics of whoever built them. Provenance records how a number was made, not whether it should exist.


20.2.6 Lineages as inheritance
Each lineage solved a version of the accountability problem, and each carries pathologies the book mostly presents as lessons rather than inheritances. Public interest law splits into a well-funded strategic tier and an overstretched front-line tier (Albiston and Nielsen 2017). Accounting’s independence norms coexisted with Arthur Andersen. Planning’s “public interest” built Robert Moses’s expressways before Davidoff (1965) tried to pluralize it. Stapleton et al. (2022) ask who benefits when a field claims the label “public interest” at all. Borrowing a profession’s methods borrows its gatekeeping and its assumptions about who gets to speak.


20.2.7 Four levels that presume the building
The book gives each lineage and genre a level of government: journalism and op-eds the city, planning and public comments the county, law and testimony the state, accounting, engineering, and reports the nation. Matching evidence and genre to the body that can act presumes that each level holds a functioning institution: a council that holds hearings, a county that reads comments, a legislature that hears testimony, an agency that reads reports. When the federal agency is the one deleting the datasets, a report to it is addressed to the eroder. When a tribal nation, an employer, a platform, or the European Union is the body that matters, the four levels have no place for it at all. They are a teaching device built for dense, functioning institutions, and they travel badly to places and moments without them.

title: 20  The Limits of the Framework
text:
20.3 From suspicion to a count
A better move than arguing borrows from Chapter 8: stop asserting and start sampling. If the book is US-centric, the cases it uses should be disproportionately American. If it prefers records to refusal, the remedies it reaches for should be disproportionately “more records.” If the four levels presume functioning governments, a large share of cases should address no government at those levels.
These are claims about a corpus, and the book is a corpus. Turning cases into rows makes every column a judgment; the tutorial makes those judgments explicit, so you can disagree with them in code rather than in vibes.

title: 20  The Limits of the Framework
section: 20.4 Tutorial: a reflexive audit of the book’s cases
text:
20.4 Tutorial: a reflexive audit of the book’s cases

20.4.1 The code book
Each row is a case the book uses as an anchor, counter-case, or worked example, with seven codes:

part: the book part where the case does its main work (I to IV; Part V holds only this chapter).
region: US, or the region of the non-US case.
level: the level of government that the case’s remedy addresses. The four levels are city, county, state, and nation, where nation means any national government, US or not. Everything else gets supranational, indigenous_nation, or non_state (a platform, employer, vendor, or network).
pressure: enclosure, exemption, or erosion.
value: openness, oversight, or ownership.
remedy: records if the book’s response is more or better records (disclosure, audits, archives, access), refusal if it is less collection, less linkage, or not building the system.
fit: clean if the pressure and value codes fit without strain, forced if you had to squeeze the case into the taxonomy.

The fit column is the reflexive move. It records the coder’s own discomfort as data.


20.4.2 The case table
The table lives inline so the audit is reproducible from this page alone.
import io
import pandas as pd

CASES = """case,part,region,level,pressure,value,remedy,fit
Reddit API pricing and Pushshift,I,US,non_state,enclosure,openness,records,clean
DSA Article 40 researcher access,I,Europe,supranational,enclosure,openness,records,clean
Boulder campaign finance,I,US,city,enclosure,openness,records,clean
Allegheny Family Screening Tool,I,US,county,exemption,oversight,records,clean
SyRI,I,Europe,nation,exemption,oversight,refusal,clean
Dutch childcare benefits scandal,I,Europe,nation,exemption,oversight,refusal,clean
EPA and NOAA dataset removals,I,US,nation,erosion,ownership,records,clean
Boulder and Denver council records,II,US,city,erosion,openness,records,clean
Machine Bias (COMPAS),II,US,county,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Pegasus Project,II,Global,nation,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Colorado Open Records Act,II,US,state,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Sandvig v. Barr (CFAA),II,US,nation,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Colorado AI Act (SB 24-205; SB 26-189),II,US,state,exemption,oversight,records,clean
NYC Local Law 144,II,US,city,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Gender Shades,II,US,non_state,exemption,oversight,records,clean
National folktables audit,II,US,nation,exemption,oversight,records,clean
EU AI Act,II,Europe,supranational,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Worker Info Exchange,II,Europe,non_state,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Robert Moses and urban renewal,II,US,city,exemption,oversight,records,forced
Boulder County Public Records Archive,II,US,county,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Central 70,II,US,state,erosion,ownership,records,forced
GetCalFresh,III,US,state,erosion,openness,records,forced
Ushahidi,III,East Africa,non_state,enclosure,openness,records,clean
Aadhaar,III,South Asia,nation,exemption,ownership,refusal,forced
Canada Algorithmic Impact Assessment,III,Canada,nation,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Federal AI procurement and inventories,III,US,nation,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Denver HMIS,III,US,county,exemption,ownership,refusal,forced
Stop LAPD Spying,III,US,city,exemption,ownership,refusal,forced
Te Mana Raraunga,III,Oceania,indigenous_nation,enclosure,ownership,refusal,forced
CARE Principles,III,Global,non_state,enclosure,ownership,refusal,forced
OCAP,III,Canada,indigenous_nation,enclosure,ownership,refusal,forced
Haugen Senate testimony,IV,US,nation,enclosure,oversight,records,clean
Colorado General Assembly testimony,IV,US,state,exemption,oversight,records,clean
Boulder County land use comment,IV,US,county,erosion,openness,records,clean
Federal rulemaking comments,IV,US,nation,erosion,oversight,records,forced
EPA Toxics Release Inventory,IV,US,nation,erosion,ownership,records,clean
"""

cases = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(CASES))
print(cases.shape)
# => (36, 8)
Thirty-six cases is not every example in the book; the selection, which favors the cases that carry the most weight in each part, is also a choice.


20.4.3 Tabulate
Start with geography, then the levels, then the remedy.
cases["us"] = cases["region"].eq("US").map({True: "US", False: "non-US"})
print(cases["us"].value_counts())
# => us
#    US        24
#    non-US    12
#    Name: count, dtype: int64

LEVELS = ["city", "county", "state", "nation"]
OTHER = ["supranational", "indigenous_nation", "non_state"]
print(pd.crosstab(cases["level"], cases["us"]).reindex(LEVELS + OTHER))
# => us                 US  non-US
#    level
#    city                5       0
#    county              5       0
#    state               5       0
#    nation              7       5
#    supranational       0       2
#    indigenous_nation   0       2
#    non_state           2       3

print(pd.crosstab(cases["us"], cases["remedy"], margins=True))
# => remedy  records  refusal  All
#    us
#    US           22        2   24
#    non-US        6        6   12
#    All          28        8   36

print(pd.crosstab(cases["part"], cases["remedy"]))
# => remedy  records  refusal
#    part
#    I             5        2
#    II           14        0
#    III           4        6
#    IV            5        0

print(pd.crosstab(cases["remedy"], cases["fit"]))
# => fit      clean  forced
#    remedy
#    records     24       4
#    refusal      2       6


20.4.4 Plot
One chart is enough. It shows where in the book refusal appears.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

tab = (pd.crosstab(cases["part"], cases["remedy"])
         .reindex(["I", "II", "III", "IV"]))
ax = tab.plot.barh(stacked=True,
                   color={"records": "#2a78d6", "refusal": "#eb6834"},
                   edgecolor="white", linewidth=2, figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("Number of cases")
ax.set_ylabel("Part of the book")
ax.set_title("Remedy the book reaches for, by part")
ax.legend(title="Remedy", frameon=False)
for side in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("remedy_by_part.png", dpi=150)
# => Parts II and IV are all blue; Part III is mostly orange.






TipThe Missing Manual



pd.crosstab and value_counts() silently drop rows whose key is missing. Suppose you could not decide how to code Aadhaar’s remedy and left the cell blank. The crosstab of us by remedy now shows eleven non-US cases instead of twelve, with no warning, and the remaining shares look tidier than your actual judgment. value_counts() hides the gap too; only value_counts(dropna=False) shows the NaN. In a reflexive audit, the cases you could not code are the most informative rows you have. Fill them explicitly (cases["remedy"].fillna("uncoded")) before you tabulate anything. A CSV looks neutral and is not: every column header is an argument.

title: 20  The Limits of the Framework
text:
20.5 What the counts reveal
Read the tables as evidence with a known sampling frame and known coder bias, not a verdict.
The book is US-centric by design and by count. Twenty-four of thirty-six cases are American. The twelve non-US cases arrive one or two per chapter, mostly as counter-cases. Every Part IV case is American: the genres teach you to write only to US bodies.
Refusal is outsourced. Only two of twenty-four US cases (Denver HMIS and Stop LAPD Spying) end in refusal; six of twelve non-US cases do. Six of the eight refusal cases sit in Part III, and the other two are Dutch counter-cases in Part I. The lineages of Part II and the genres of Part IV contain none. The book files refusal under what its neighbors say, not what its professions do, and borrows most of it from elsewhere: Dutch courts, Māori and First Nations governance, global Indigenous data networks. The introduction admitted this in prose; the table shows its shape.
Refusal does not fit the taxonomy. Six of the eight refusal cases were coded forced, against four of twenty-eight records cases. When a case’s answer is “do not collect,” the coder had to stretch “ownership” to cover it and invent a pressure (usually “enclosure”) that the community itself might reject. Te Mana Raraunga does not describe Māori data as enclosed; it describes it as Māori. The framework’s vocabulary has no native word for that.
The four levels do not hold the world. The US cases spread almost evenly across the levels (five city, five county, five state, seven nation), but that evenness measures the book’s own rule for assigning lineages and genres to levels, not the world. Coding any national government as nation lets five non-US cases sit on the levels, yet none of them reaches a Part IV genre. Nine of thirty-six cases address no government at the four levels at all: five non-state actors (two of them American, the Reddit API and Gender Shades), two supranational regimes, and two Indigenous nations.
Labor and measurement are absent because they were never columns. No code records who did the work or whether the measure was valid. That absence is the most important finding and the hardest to see, because a table counts only what its code book names. Exercise 20.2 asks you to add the columns.
None of this refutes the framework. It locates it. Neff et al. (2017) argue that critical data studies and data science improve each other only when critique is practiced inside the work. A framework that ships with its own audit, and invites you to recode it, is doing that.






NoteIn the Public Interest



This chapter is about ownership of the framework itself. Someone owns the framework’s definitions: what counts as a “record,” which pressures have names, which levels of government count. Ownership in the sense of Chapter 5 means stewardship with duties to beneficiaries, and the beneficiaries of a framework are the communities it is applied to. The specific claim: the reflexive audit is a stewardship tool only if its code book is open to revision by the people being coded. A case table that Te Mana Raraunga or Worker Info Exchange could not edit is a records-first instrument describing refusal from the outside. Opening the code book (literally, as a pull request to this book) is how the framework’s ownership becomes shared rather than declared.

title: 20  The Limits of the Framework
text:
20.6 Exercises
Exercise 20.1 (Guided). Run the audit exactly as written and confirm the tables match. Then recode three cases you disagree with (for example, is the Haugen testimony really enclosure? Is the Colorado AI Act’s remedy only records?). Rerun every table. In 300 words, report which shares changed and whether any finding in “What the counts reveal” reverses. Save as exercises/ch20_recode.md.
Exercise 20.2 (Guided). Add two columns the code book lacks: labor (who does the maintenance work the case depends on: paid_staff, volunteer, contract, affected_community, or unknown) and measure_contested (yes if the case turns on whether a measure is valid). Code all thirty-six cases, using unknown honestly. Tabulate both. In 300 words, explain what the new columns reveal that the original seven concealed.
Exercise 20.3 (Runnable, real public data). Clone the book’s public repository (https://github.com/cuinfoscience/Public-Interest-Data-Science-Book) and use pandas to count, for every ch-*.qmd file, mentions of a list of jurisdictions you choose (for example “Colorado”, “Netherlands”, “India”, “Kenya”, “Aotearoa”, “Brazil”). Produce a chapter-by-jurisdiction table. Compare it with the tutorial’s hand-coded table. Where do mention counts and case codes disagree, and which better measures “US-centric”?
Exercise 20.4 (Open-ended). Pick one of the seven limits and draft a one-page proposal for the chapter-scale revision the book would need to address it: the new section’s argument, one non-US or refusal-first anchor case, a tutorial sketch, and three sources. If you want the revision to reach the book, open it as a pull request.
Exercise 20.5 (Open-ended: critical-reflection memo). Write a 500-word critical-reflection memo on a piece of public interest data work you have produced, such as an artifact from a Part IV chapter. Answer four questions. First, whose interests does the work serve, and whose might it harm? Name groups, not abstractions. Second, which affected communities were not consulted, and why not? “Time” is an answer only if you say what consultation would have required. Third, where does the framework fail for this case? Code your own piece with the tutorial’s code book; if any column was forced, say why. Fourth, what would you do with more time, and what would you decide not to do? If you deposit the work (Chapter 19), put the memo in the deposit so the reflection travels with the artifact.

title: 20  The Limits of the Framework
text:
20.7 Closing the book
The book began with a few lines of Python against the Wikimedia pageviews API and a claim that “public interest” is an operational question rather than a slogan. It ends with a count of the book’s own blind spots and a memo about where your work falls short. That sequence is the practice: build the record, then audit the record, including the one you built.
The framework will change. The next version should start from more places than Boulder, take refusal as a first move rather than a neighbor’s idea, count the people who keep the records alive, and admit that the four levels of government are a scaffold, not a law of nature. Some of those revisions will come from readers; the repository accepts pull requests.
Until then, the work is the same as it was on page one. Find the pressure. Name the value. Build the installed base that lets the value last, and ask, every time, who it is for and who it leaves out. Then deposit what you made, so that the next public, the one that will argue with you, can find it.

title: Appendix A — Appendix A: AI Assistance Disclosure
text:
A.1 What was AI-assisted
Draft zero of this book was produced with substantial assistance from Claude, an assistant made by Anthropic. The assistant generated first-pass prose for the original twenty-two chapters and the index, following a detailed editorial prompt written by the author. The author then reviewed, revised, and (in many places) rewrote the output. The book’s framework, chapter scope, running examples, and exercise design originate with the author. The prose does not.
The 2027 revisions were also AI-assisted. Working from the author’s course design for INFO 4871/5871 (Spring 2027) and the author’s article on public interest data infrastructuring, Claude first reorganized the book into course modules and then, at the author’s direction, regrouped it by theme: it paired each pressure with its value in a single chapter, expanded the installed-base chapter with its intellectual predecessors, revised framing, cases, levels of government, and exercises, moved tutorials between chapters, and drafted the new chapter on the limits of the framework. Those revisions are under author review. Commits from them are marked in the repository history, and new bibliography entries are flagged for verification.
This disclosure exists because a book about public interest data science should not hide how it was made. The same principle that asks a model card to document training data asks an author to document drafting practice.

title: Appendix A — Appendix A: AI Assistance Disclosure
text:
A.2 What was not AI-assisted
The bibliography’s selection reflects the author’s reading, not the assistant’s. The running examples (Boulder and Denver municipal records, a synthetic worker-log fixture, a class-wide FOIA tracker, the regulations.gov walkthrough) are authorial choices grounded in the companion course. The “Missing Manual” and “In the Public Interest” callout convention is the author’s. The genre structure, and particularly its commitment to producing submittable artifacts, is the author’s pedagogical argument.
The assistant was asked not to invent citations. Where a suggested reference could not be verified, the bibliography flags the entry for follow-up rather than recording a fabricated one. Readers who find a citation that cannot be located should open an issue.

title: Appendix A — Appendix A: AI Assistance Disclosure
text:
A.3 How to verify

The prompt used to generate draft zero is preserved in the repository’s issue history under the label prompt-archive.
Each chapter’s first commit is the AI-generated draft. Later commits include human revisions and the AI-assisted 2027 restructure; commit messages say which. Use git log --follow ch-NN-slug.qmd to inspect a chapter’s editorial history.
Chapter-by-chapter revision notes are maintained in claude.md and in pull-request discussions.

title: Appendix A — Appendix A: AI Assistance Disclosure
text:
A.4 Why disclose
Because readers deserve to know. Because other authors deciding whether to use similar tools need honest reports of what worked and what did not. Because a book that argues for documentation of automated systems must document its own use of one. And because the professional lineages this book draws on (journalism, law, accounting, planning, engineering) all insist on provenance: whose work, whose hand, whose judgment.

B.1 Cross-cutting tools
This appendix collects external resources for readers who want to go further. Each chapter has its own curated “Further Reading and Resources” section; those lists are the place to start. This appendix aggregates the cross-cutting tools, communities, and training venues that appear in more than one chapter, plus a few that did not fit anywhere.

title: Appendix B — Appendix B: Further Resources
text:
Datasette (datasette.io). Simon Willison’s toolkit for publishing SQLite databases as inspectable web applications. Used in Chapters 3, 7, 8, and 19.

The Wayback Machine (archive.org/web). The Internet Archive’s web capture service. Used in Chapters 5 and 19.
regulations.gov (regulations.gov). The federal rulemaking docket. Central to Chapter 18.
DMPTool (dmptool.org). Templates for data management plans. Central to Chapter 16.
Zenodo (zenodo.org). CERN’s general-purpose research archive. Central to Chapter 19.
fairlearn (fairlearn.org). Python toolkit for disaggregated performance evaluation. Central to Chapters 8 and 10.
geopandas (geopandas.org). Geographic data for pandas users. Central to Chapter 9.

section: B.4 Critical readings you did not meet in this book
text:
B.4 Critical readings you did not meet in this book
This book’s framework focuses on records, openness, oversight, and ownership. Readers who want a sharper critique of that framing should start with:

Simone Browne, Dark Matters: On the Surveillance of Blackness (2015)
Ruha Benjamin, Race After Technology (2019)
Safiya Umoja Noble, Algorithms of Oppression (2018)
Sasha Costanza-Chock, Design Justice (2020)
Audra Simpson, Mohawk Interruptus (2014) on refusal as political stance

These texts do not fit neatly into the chapter arc because they do not accept its premises. That is the point of reading them.

B.5 When things change
External links break. Tools deprecate. APIs change. Report a broken link or a deprecated tool by opening an issue against the book’s repository. Maintenance of this appendix is the point, not an afterthought.
